articles.title_orig: The World is His Oyster
articles.title_zh: The World is His Oyster
articles.content_orig:
October 8, 2026 | Claire Hall
Seafood entrepreneur Keegan Jalbert is developing a new approach to oyster feed
Graduate student Keegan Jalbert, left, and his brother-in-law Bryan Zambrano are pictured on a boat as they visit an aquaculture farm in Ecuador, where they discussed feed trials using AccessFlora's proprietary omega-3 feed. Jalbert's startup is one of the finalists in next week's Wolff New Venture Competition (UConn Today).
Graduate student Keegan Jalbert ’23 (CLAS) ’27 MS has always been interested in agriculture, food, and innovation. Today he is finding new ways to grow oysters and share his love of seafood with customers who live far from the ocean.
Jalbert is the founder of AccessFlora , a sustainable aquaculture company with a proprietary omega-3 aquafeed for raising oysters in purified water at a hatchery. The outcome is a larger and healthier shellfish that isn’t confined to the coast nor dependent upon favorable ocean conditions.
“I think what keeps me going as an entrepreneur is that this work is very fun,’’ says Jalbert, who is pursuing a master’s degree in nutritional science. “My greatest motivation is the impact on how we source omega-3s as a critical nutrient for our human health and for agriculture. What’s helped me so much with the startup is that I love my work, and because of it I’ve developed great personal connections.’’
Startup to Compete in Wolff New Venture Championship
AccessFlora is one of five UConn-affiliated startups participating in the Wolff New Venture Competition next Tuesday, Oct. 13, at Pratt & Whitney Stadium at Rentschler Field in East Hartford.
The competition, now in its 11th year, is hosted by the Connecticut Center for Entrepreneurship and Innovation (CCEI) . The event will include awards of more than $150,000, including a $40,000 grand prize for the first-place finisher. Jalbert says whatever money AccessFlora wins will help ramp up production.
“In terms of shellfish farming, yes, what we’re doing is revolutionary,’’ Jalbert says. “Shellfish are not raised in land-based aquaculture because the omega-3 feed would be too expensive. On one hand, that makes shellfish really great, because they can grow out in the ocean without being fed and they are great for the environment. But on the other hand, this cultivation method takes a long time, it is labor intensive, and it is vulnerable to unpredictable ocean conditions. While our technology will not replace traditional shellfish farming, it does provide a highly resilient and quick way to raise oysters, independent of ocean access, allowing this to be done inland.’’
“The way that this technology works is that we have a healthy microalgae that we use to convert vinegar into omega-3 in controlled conditions, kind of like yeast turns sugars into alcohol,’’ Jalbert says. “This gives us a clean DHA omega-3, the nutrient that makes seafood such an important part in our diet.’’
But that’s just one step for the company.
“Our longer-term plan is for this to not just be raising oysters, but to be serving as an omega-3 source in enriched/fortified plant-based foods,’’ Jalbert says. “This is because that is a large market that our technology is really well suited for, especially now that the majority of U.S. population is deficient in omega-3.’’
Jalbert Brings Extensive Experience to His Work
Jalbert’s startup won the 2025 Innovation Quest competition at UConn and a $15,000 grand prize. He has partnered with professor Mingyu Qiao, in the Department of Nutritional Sciences in the College of Agriculture, Health and Natural Resources, who is a leader and innovator in sustainable food systems.
In addition, Jalbert took advantage of UConn’s co-op program and worked with both the Boston Beer Company, in new product development, and as a microbiology intern at the U.S. Department of Energy. Through exchange programs, he has learned about shellfish aquaculture in Melbourne, Australia, Manabi, Ecuador, as well as here in Connecticut.
Summer Accelerator: ‘I Must Have Learned 100 Things’
Part of Jalbert’s entrepreneurial journey included attending CCEI’s eight-week Summer Accelerator, which offers promising startups $15,000 in non-dilutive funding, mentorship, access to masterclasses and workshops, and pro-bono legal, accounting, marketing, product development, and banking services.
“Summer Accelerator is like a summer camp for startups,’’ Jalbert says. “It packs a lot into eight weeks. This summer we were testing how we can distribute our omega-3 product and learning the cost structures and economics of getting product to customers. I must have learned 100 things during Summer Accelerator, but the biggest thing was unit economics and cost structure of bringing the product to market.’’
With the oyster feed gaining traction, AccessFlora is focusing on educating people on the seafood nutrient. Jalbert just hired his first employee to work on business outreach. “We are in real talks with restaurants and agricultural experts,’’ he says.
AccessFlora also manages a food trailer, called Reef-to-Table, which caters weddings and other events. Although that isn’t the primary focus of the business, it is a terrific outlet for Jalbert.
“It’s a good way of having direct interactions with consumers. I enjoy it so much,’’ he says. “I have to be conscience of my time commitments, but if it could be my weekend hobby, I’d do it. The raw bar business is a ton of fun and already profitable.”
The Wolff New Venture Competition will be held on Tuesday (Oct. 13) at Pratt and Whitney Stadium at Rentschler Field in East Hartford from 5 to 9 p.m. The event is free to attend and all are welcome. Pre-registration is required at https://luma.com/i2690pqa .
The Wolff New Venture Competition is supported by the generosity of the Wolff Family as well as wiggin(x), Fiondella, Milone & LaSaracina LLP, Sardilli Produce and Dairy Co., Prime Materials Recovery Inc., Big Bang, Baystate Financial, Webster Bank, Mark and Jamie Summers, Putnam Plastics, Eric Marziali, Bob and Linda Delisle, Dick and Carol Stewart and Event Resources.

articles.content_orig:
Campaign aims to raise more than $45,000 on Oct. 16, 2026, in support of organic integrity
LAKEWOOD, Colo. , Oct. 8, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- In recognition of World Food Day on Oct. 16, Natural Grocers ® , the nation's leading family-operated organic and natural grocery retailer, will once again host a one-day, in-store fundraising campaign benefiting The Cornucopia Institute. Natural Grocers has pledged to donate 1% of sales from all stores nationwide, with a goal of raising more than $45,000 for the nonprofit.
SUPPORTING ORGANIC INTEGRITY TOGETHER Customers are invited to shop at their local Natural Grocers on Oct. 16 to participate in the company's second annual World Food Day fundraiser for The Cornucopia Institute. 1% of the day's sales will be donated to support the organization's work to safeguard the integrity of organic labeling, production, processing and marketing.
"World Food Day reminds us that everyday choices at the grocery store can help shape the future of food," said Raquel Isely, vice president of marketing at Natural Grocers. "We are proud to continue our support of The Cornucopia Institute and its important work to protect organic integrity for generations to come."
THE CORNUCOPA INSTITUTE The Cornucopia Institute is a nonprofit watchdog for organic food and a trusted resource for organic advocates seeking to align their purchases with their values. Through consumer tools, policy work, and investigations into the organic marketplace, Cornucopia works to uncover the truth behind organic food and advocate for an organic label consumers and retailers can trust.
Cornucopia Executive Director Melody Morrell says, "Natural Grocers is turning a single day of shopping into a powerful investment in our food future. Together, we are driving demand for the best organic food, ensuring tomorrow's innovative organic brands have a chance, and keeping dedicated organic farmers on the land."
ABOUT NATURAL GROCERS BY VITAMIN COTTAGE Founded in 1955, Natural Grocers by Vitamin Cottage, Inc. (NYSE: NGVC ) is an expanding specialty retailer of natural and organic groceries, body care products and dietary supplements. The grocery products sold by Natural Grocers must meet strict quality guidelines and may not contain artificial flavors, preservatives or sweeteners (as defined by its standards), synthetic colors or partially hydrogenated or hydrogenated oils. The Company sells only USDA-certified organic produce and exclusively pasture-raised, non-confinement dairy products and free-range eggs. Natural Grocers' flexible smaller-store format allows it to offer affordable prices in a shopper-friendly, clean and convenient retail environment. The Company also provides extensive free science-based Nutrition Education programs to help customers and Crew make informed health and nutrition choices. Natural Grocers is committed to its Five Founding Principles —including its "Commitment to Community" and "Commitment to Crew." In fiscal year 2025, the Company invested more than $16 million in incremental compensation and discretionary payments for Crew. Headquartered in Lakewood, CO, Natural Grocers has 175 stores in 22 states. Visit naturalgrocers.com for more information and store locations.
THE CORNUCOPIA INSTITUTE The Cornucopia Institute is a tax-exempt, charitable organization incorporated in 2004. Its work is supported primarily through individual donor contributions from farmers and consumers. They do not solicit or receive any government funds. The Cornucopia Institute is your watchdog, bringing you the truth behind organic. This nonprofit charity partners with independent retailers and co-ops to share and amplify tools that grow demand for the best organic farms and brands. Follow them on Facebook , Instagram , BlueSky and YouTube .

articles.title_orig: Alabama’s Prehistoric Past: Fossils Reveal a World That Existed Millions of Years Ago
articles.title_zh: Alabama’s Prehistoric Past: Fossils Reveal a World That Existed Millions of Years Ago
articles.content_orig:
by Brian White, Ashonti Ford
When most people think about dinosaur fossils, they may picture the wide-open landscapes of Montana, Wyoming or the Dakotas.
But some of the most significant fossil discoveries in the country are much closer to home — right here in Alabama.
Inside the Birmingham Mcwane Center, thousands of fossils are stored just feet away from visitors, offering a glimpse into an Alabama that existed long before the state — or even humans — were here.
Behind collection-room doors, row after row of cabinets hold bones, teeth and other remnants of life dating back more than half a billion years.
June Ebersole, director of collections at McWane Science Center, oversees about half a million specimens, including fossils found nowhere else in the world.
“A lot of people think you have to go out west to find fossils,” Ebersole said. “But what my research is showing is that Alabama, by far, is the number one state in the U.S. in terms of paleo-biodiversity.”
The collection spans an extraordinary stretch of time.
“We have fossils here that are over 500 million years old, to some that are just from the Ice Age, only 12,000 to 14,000 years old, and everything in between,” Ebersole said. “We have so many fossils here, I’m discovering new species all the time.”
Among the most remarkable specimens is one that helped change what scientists knew about dinosaurs in the eastern United States.
Ebersole opens a drawer containing the remains of Eotrachodon orientalis, a newly identified species of duck-billed dinosaur.
The fossils may look like a pile of bones to the untrained eye, but together they represent the most complete dinosaur ever found in the eastern half of the United States, with about 60% of its skeleton recovered.
And the discovery was made not in a remote western desert, but in Montgomery County.
“It’s from Montgomery County, right on the side of the creek, just outside the city limits,” Ebersole said. “This is the only one of this particular species in the world.”
The dinosaur is only part of Alabama’s prehistoric story.
The McWane collection also includes fossils of sharks, turtles and birds, along with a 315-million-year-old dragonfly wing discovered in Walker County.
Thousands of fossil shark teeth fill drawers inside the collection, including one massive collection from the time of the dinosaurs.
“It is literally — here’s 10,000 fossil goblin shark teeth,” Ebersole said. “It’s one of the biggest collections of these on the planet.”
Most visitors to the science center will see only a fraction of the collection.
But behind the scenes, scientists continue studying the specimens and making discoveries that help reconstruct the world that existed beneath Alabama millions of years ago.
Long before 250 years of American history, Alabama was already writing a story of its own — one measured not in centuries, but in hundreds of millions of years.
And today, pieces of that ancient story remain carefully preserved, waiting to reveal what Alabama looked like long before any of us arrived.

articles.title_orig: Top Climate Scientists Set Out Five Steps to Help the World Prepare for Super El NiñO | Newswise
articles.title_zh: Top Climate Scientists Set Out Five Steps to Help the World Prepare for Super El NiñO | Newswise
articles.content_orig:
Newswise — Researchers have identified five key ways countries across the globe can be better prepared for the impending El Niño – and reduce its potentially devastating toll on human health.
The call to action , led by the University of Bristol and published in The Lancet , highlights how although it is widely-acknowledged El Niño exacerbates wide-ranging health risks posed by climate change, the additional threats presented remain largely unquantified. The researchers emphasise that as the El Niño cycle can be forecasted months in advance, preparatory measures should be put in place to mitigate the impact, especially in countries most vulnerable.
Study lead author Dr Ruby Lieber, Senior Research Associate in Climate Science at the University of Bristol, said: “We know the number of people affected by climate-related disasters is strongly influenced by the El Niño cycle, but there is little evidence available establishing how much of the health burden can be attributed to climate change and how much was driven by El Niño.
“Since the current El Niño pushes many regions into more extreme climates, there’s a pressing and unprecedented need to better understand, measure and pinpoint the different dangers for individual countries and places.”
The study recommends five important actions to gain this comprehensive risk overview, which holds the key to being able to tackle and minimise the likely consequences, including the spread of infectious diseases, malnutrition, and various heat-related conditions such as dehydration and heatstroke.
Dr Lieber said: “These steps will require greater collaboration between climate and health researchers and, equally fundamental, concerted action between research funders, the World Health Organization (WHO), the wider UN system, the World Bank, and non-governmental organisations.
“Partnership working is imperative and such global entities need to urgently call on advances in attribution science to more accurately recognise and assess how much of the repercussions are the result of human-induced climate change and how much are a result of El Niño. By isolating the El Niño-related impacts, we can generate much more targeted and event-specific actions.”
A significant El Niño, which describes the warming of sea surface temperature, is likely to occur towards the end of this year with some forecasts predicting the strongest event on record. The direct effects of El Niño will be felt across the globe and may heighten instances of extreme weather in regions such as India, East Asia, South America, parts of Africa and the West Pacific.
Co-author Dann Mitchell, Shanta Professorial Chair in Planetary Health at the University of Bristol, added: “It’s clear that we cannot afford to ignore this emerging threat, which poses potentially devastating but predictable risks to communities around the world.
“Climate and health researchers must unite, with the full backing of national and international agencies, to create a much more advanced evidence base. This will enable us to ramp up global resilience and implement adaptation strategies to mitigate the many deeply concerning health implications, particularly for countries more acutely exposed.”

articles.title_orig: PepsiCo beats earnings expectations, lowers guidance as it aims to stabilize North America business
articles.title_zh: PepsiCo beats earnings expectations, lowers guidance as it aims to stabilize North America business
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
PepsiCo ( PEP ) posted third quarter results that beat Wall Street's expectations on Thursday but lowered its profit outlook as the company works to regain momentum in the US market.
"We continue to operate with a high sense of urgency to sustainably improve the company's financial and marketplace performance (most notably in North America)," PepsiCo CEO Ramon Laguarta said in prepared remarks.
PepsiCo's revenue grew 5.6% year over year to $25.27 billion, just beating the Street's expectations of roughly $25 billion. Adjusted earnings per share came in at $2.34, slightly higher than the $2.29 per share expected, per Bloomberg consensus data.
Tariff refunds totaled $178 million in the third quarter, benefiting the beverage business, executives said.
For fiscal year 2026, the company now expects net revenue to come in at the high end of its range, up approximately 6%. But PepsiCo lowered its forecast for core earnings per share growth to 2.5%-3%, down from the low end of a 5%-7% range.
The stock rose by about 1% in early trading following the results.
The company said it saw results from innovation around portion control, multipack offerings, protein, fiber, and simpler ingredients, with strong performance from its NKD, Doritos Protein, and Lays Baked with Olive Oil products. On the beverage side, lower-sugar Gatorade and zero-sugar Pepsi Treats drove results.
However, the company reiterated its plans to raise prices by 15% this year to offset higher input costs. Earlier this year, Pepsi lowered prices, which led its North America core operating margin to decline by 280 basis points.
The company said the price reduction led to positive volume, unit growth, and share gains in its US snacks business, following low-single-digit volume declines.
The return to growth gives "flexibility … to absorb this new wave of inflation that is coming to every country, not only the US, given energy prices and given agricultural prices," he said, "We're putting some guardrails to our people, making sure that next year's pricing is going to be below [25%]."
The company doesn't expect inflation pressures to end anytime soon, as "commodities continue to ramp up," CFO Stephen Schmitt told investors.
Laguarta told investors that the company is also working to cut costs and hinted at potential layoffs.
"Additional structural cost reduction actions are being identified and will be implemented in the coming months to help fund investments that aim to accelerate organic revenue growth and mitigate the impacts of rising input cost inflation," Laguarta said.
Executives didn't dismiss the idea of another acquisition following the $2 billion takeover of Poppi in 2025.
"We've been looking at that for quite some time, both in foods and beverages," Laguarta said. "We keep looking at opportunities to complete the portfolio, smaller tuck-in opportunities … We never say no if it has strategic value, it has financial returns, and it makes sense for the levers of growth that we can provide."
RBC Capital Markets managing director Nik Modi said there are no "overnight fixes" to right Pepsi's ship.
"Consumer staples is in a tough spot," he said. "Anywhere you slice or dice it, they're going to have to make some tough choices over the next 6 to 12 months."

articles.title_orig: He planned to become a philosopher. Then he found New Orleans’ startup world.
articles.title_zh: He planned to become a philosopher. Then he found New Orleans’ startup world.
articles.content_orig:
In college, Andrew Albert imagined a career in academia. He’d get global experience, earn a PhD in philosophy, come back to start a think tank in New Orleans and shape public policy in his hometown.
In the end, he did build a career that contributes to New Orleans — but in the city’s startup ecosystem.
He’s now programs director at the Idea Village , where he leads the team responsible for its accelerators, thought leadership and marketing and communications.
“What does it mean to be Black in the South and wrestle with institutions and power?”
His path there included working at New Orleans software startup Lucid during its $60 million Series B, before it became New Orleans’ first tech unicorn. He went on to support founders through Venture for America , co-found River Basin Distillery and later launch Exclave Spirits .
In this edition of How I Got Here , Albert talked about trading academia for startups, the job he considers his “working MBA” and what people hoping to build companies should know.
This Q&A has been edited for length and clarity.
Being Black from New Orleans, it was like: Go be a lawyer, go be a doctor. Those are the traditional pathways. So I started my undergrad career at Loyola University New Orleans as a bio major. I was like, “Oh, cool. I guess I’ll go become a doctor.”
But because Loyola is a Jesuit university, all freshmen take Intro to Philosophy. I had a chem lab with no windows and fluorescent lights, and then I went to this philosophy class with these very heady questions. It was incredibly appealing.
I literally dropped everything within that semester and switched to philosophy.
A lot of my undergraduate career was spent studying dynamics of power, specifically racial power. What does it mean to be Black in the South and wrestle with institutions and power? How might you see yourself in the world?
I had every intention of being a full-time academic. I had an amazing mentor who suggested I get a master’s degree first to figure out whether grad school was really what I wanted.
I’d had a Fulbright experience in the UK and fell in love with London. I was also a super nerd. You hear the stories about James Baldwin and the intellectual expat, and I knew I wanted to do something abroad.
So I went to the London School of Economics to study philosophy and public policy.
I immediately got to grad school and was like, “I do not like this at all.”
Before that, my ambition was to get a PhD, make policy recommendations, yada yada yada, solve the world’s problems. That was my very naive educational journey.
I knew fairly quickly that my educational journey was going to stop at the master’s level. In retrospect, that was probably a great thing because it gave me time to reflect on what I actually wanted to do.
A core driver for me was: How might I participate within the city of New Orleans in some productive fashion? Originally, I thought it was policy. I realized I didn’t want to do that.
This was the golden age of startups, and I was living in East London, where there was a lot of buzz and excitement around them.
One option was Venture for America, a fellowship for recent grads who wanted to work at high-growth startups. I applied, got accepted and really put all my eggs in the “I’m working in New Orleans” basket.
Thinking back on it, I had this singular idea: Whatever the best company in the world is, that’s the company I’m going to work for.
Plan B was to do Plan A for me.
I was fortunate enough to land that role at Lucid.
My title was executive analyst, but I worked there essentially in a chief of staff role. I did everything from financial planning and analysis and board governance to designing a 35,000-sq.-ft.office space. If there was a job that needed to be done and there wasn’t a full-time hire to do it, it was my role.
My time at Lucid was very much my working MBA. We raised a $60 million Series B, which in New Orleans was a massive amount of capital. I got to work with bankers.
I remember the CEO at the time telling me, “The amount of access that you’re going to get here far surpasses what you’re supposed to have, and it is going to completely warp how you move through your profession.”
Then I pivoted away from operationally working in startups and went back to what I was interested in from school: economic development.
I ended up working for Venture for America. First, I was director of New Orleans, and then I became VP of venture growth, where I spent most of my time building our venture growth department, essentially the entrepreneurship department.
I helped design how we supported fellows and alumni on their entrepreneurial journeys, ran our accelerator and all of our entrepreneurial programming. It really was like 1-800-founder for the better part of six and a half years.
Around 2017 or 2018, I read the story of Nearest Green and Uncle Nearest Whiskey. I remember thinking, “God damn, why didn’t I come up with this? This is amazing.”
After those emotions went away, the next thing was: This is actually a global Black story that can and should be told. This isn’t just an American Black story.
That seed eventually became part of Exclave Spirits, which tells a broader story of how Black people have contributed to distilled spirits.
Actually building something changed how I work with founders. It’s the difference between theory and practice.
By building something, I was able to cut out the jargon and get to the foundational principles of what it means to build a business.
The hard part is being able to assess risk, anticipate things and make very tight resource decisions. You hear stories of investors pushing, pushing, pushing, and founders losing sight of why they got into it in the first place.
My approach is: I don’t know exactly what you’re going through. This shit is hard. It’s lonely. It’s winding. But I try to be the friendly voice saying, “All right, I know it’s hard, but keep pushing.”
Being perpetually curious is something you can develop and always work on.
Be comfortable with pivoting, because everything we put on a whiteboard sounds great to ourselves. The minute you take a step forward, you’re going to face something that forces you to change.
There’s the “fail fast” adage. I switch it to: Be able to pivot and rebound fast.
The other thing is to be very diligent with how you question your customers. You can build something great, something technologically ahead of everybody else. Awesome. But what I always go back to is: Will somebody give you money for it repeatedly?
If not, you kind of just have a science project, which is cool. But at the core of it, a business is: You create value that somebody pays you for.
And what’s the worst that could happen?
The cost of building is as low as it’s probably ever been. To the extent that you see a problem, see a challenge, take a shot. What’s the worst thing that’s going to happen?

articles.title_orig: A Vail mountaineer is vying to be the first American woman to scale the world's tallest volcanoes
articles.title_zh: A Vail mountaineer is vying to be the first American woman to scale the world's tallest volcanoes
articles.content_orig:
In August 2024, Vail’s Nicole Otake climbed Papua New Guinea’s Mount Giluwe, the highest volcano in Oceania.
Getting there required the kind of logistics that adventurous travelers love: “A guy picked us up at the airport, then handed us off to another guy and his son who connected us to someone else,” Otake said.
This story first appeared in The Outsider , the premium outdoor newsletter by Jason Blevins. In it, he covers the industry from the inside out, plus the fun side of being outdoors in our beautiful state.
Eventually, Otake and her climbing partner were led to a few men on the side of a road in Papua New Guinea’s Western Highlands where they all began a two-day trek toward the mountain. The men were barefoot and carried handmade spears.
Giluwe rises 14,327 feet — not especially high by mountaineering standards — but the climb was muddy, wet and remote. Along the way, Otake saw enormous prehistoric-looking birds running through the highlands.
“It was like being back in time,” Otake said. “It was super remote and super cool.”
It was also the fourth stop on a checklist: climbing the Seven Volcanic Summits, the highest volcanoes on each continent.
Otake, 32, has so far summited six of the seven. All that remains is Mount Sidley in Antarctica, the most remote of the seven and by far the most expensive to reach. If Otake gets there, she will become the first American woman to complete the Seven Volcanic Summits.
Otake started climbing mountains because she liked the idea of a challenge she could quantify. She is analytical and she likes spreadsheets and lists. The Seven Volcanic Summits gave her all three — along with a reason to start learning how to climb increasingly big and remote mountains.
Then, the mountains started leading her somewhere she hadn’t expected. From one summit, she would look across a valley and see another peak — one that wasn’t on any list, wasn’t particularly well known and, in some cases, was rarely climbed.
“Now there are so many mountains that aren’t on any of these lists that are so much higher on my list,” she said.
That shift — from checking off summits to seeking out remote mountains for their own sake — has also changed the way Otake thinks about mountaineering. She has learned how expensive and complicated mountaineering can be, and how much knowledge it takes to get into the mountains without paying someone else to handle everything. She has also learned that the sport is still overwhelmingly male and that many aspiring climbers, particularly women, lack the mentorship and resources she wished she had.
So this year, after losing the remote leadership job that had helped finance her climbing, Otake started Ash to Altitude, a small logistics company designed to help people plan their own expeditions — without the luxury price tag.
“I really believe people need access to these mountains,” she said.
Otake’s first big mountain — also one of the Seven Volcanic Summits — was Kilimanjaro, which she climbed in March 2023 in less than three days.
She had always been interested in volcanoes. Her father was born in Hawaii before it became a state , and because of that Otake grew up with a connection to the islands and the volcanoes that shape them. As she learned more about volcanoes around the world, she came across the Seven Volcanic Summits.
Learning that no American woman had completed the seven gave her new motivation.
“Someone will always be stronger or faster,” Otake said. “But you can’t take away the first of something.”
At first, the goal was simply to complete the list. But as Otake and her husband, Rocco, planned and executed the expeditions, they got hooked on going higher and farther. Rocco was also interested in climbing the traditional Seven Summits, the highest mountain on each continent, and the two began taking on bigger objectives together. In the process, Otake became the person handling the logistics.
“It lets my spreadsheet brain be happy,” she said.
The more mountains they climbed — like Denali and Mount Elbrus and Pico de Orizaba — the more the list became a gateway into alpine climbing. Each expedition taught them something about planning, logistics and what they were capable of taking on next. Ticking boxes became less and less important.
“Starting with a list has given us the skills and tools to become better mountaineers,” Otake said. “It was a good way to start because I wasn’t sure of anything else. But now there are so many mountains that aren’t on any of these lists that are so much more intriguing.”
Like Alpamayo in Peru, which she calls the most beautiful mountain in the world.
Even that experience, Otake said, made her want to look beyond the mountain she was climbing.
“But as we’re climbing that, it’s like, look across the valley and there’s Artesonraju , which is even more beautiful,” she said. “So now we’re going back next June.”
That curiosity has pushed Otake toward increasingly remote and self-supported objectives. She and Rocco have learned how to arrange their own transportation, permits, lodging, food and acclimatization rather than simply signing up for a commercial expedition and showing up at the trailhead.
Otake likes that part almost as much as the climbing.
She and Rocco live full time in a solar-powered van, spending much of the winter in the Vail Valley and leaving in the summer to climb. The van is minimalist: Otake says she owns one dress and one pair of heels, which both live crammed into a wheel well, while the couple’s climbing and skiing gear occupies the remaining space.
The setup suits a life organized around mountains. When she’s not climbing, Otake is usually planning the next climb — researching routes, comparing costs, figuring out transportation and finding people on the ground who can help them navigate places they have never been.
The process has given Otake a crash course in the barriers to mountaineering — not just the physical ones, but the financial and logistical ones, too. She has learned how much it costs to get to these places, how difficult it can be to know whom to trust and how much easier the process becomes if someone else has already figured it out.
The more time she spent in the mountains, the more Otake also noticed how difficult it can be for someone else to get started. Mountaineering is expensive. There is the gear, the international travel, the time required for training and acclimatization, and, for many mountains, thousands of dollars paid to an expedition company to arrange the logistics and guide the climb.
Otake had been fortunate. For four and a half years, she worked in leadership at Act Blue, a digital fundraising platform that builds open-access software for Democratic campaigns, progressive organizations, and 501(c)(3) organizations. The remote role allowed her to take extended time away for climbing. She bought her van and most of her equipment and learned how to organize increasingly complicated expeditions herself. “I was really lucky,” she said.
So, when Otake lost that job in May of 2025, she decided to try her hand at professionalizing something she already knew how to do.
In February, she started Ash to Altitude, a small expedition-planning company that helps climbers arrange their own trips. The idea is to work directly with local operators and strip away the overhead of a fully packaged expedition. Because Otake has already done so many expeditions herself, she knows how much they can cost — versus how much is often charged. She said she has seen companies charge about $7,000 for an Elbrus expedition that she can organize for roughly $3,000, including flights and a visa.
“It drives me crazy to see people exploit other people, especially to go to parts of the world where they can’t promote local pricing,” she says.
The business is still small — so far, many of her clients have come through friends and Instagram — but the idea extends beyond saving money. Otake wants to make the information and experience she has accumulat

articles.title_orig: Chinese militia boat spotted for first time off Taiwan's Pacific coast
articles.title_zh: Chinese militia boat spotted for first time off Taiwan's Pacific coast
articles.content_orig:
A vessel, which APEX Aviation says is Chinese fishing boat Minfudingyu 07902 is seen off Taiwan's east coast in mid-August 2026 | Photo: APEX Aviation/Handout via REUTERS
A militia craft from China was recorded with two other ships off Taiwan's Pacific coast in August, according to Reuters , the first such sighting. The ship, identified in an Apex Aviation report seen by Reuters as the Minfudingyu 07902, is a fishing boat that serves as a militia vessel. It was sailing along with a coast guard cutter and a research ship.
China has raised east-coast patrols since June and claims the island. Officials in Taiwan call this blockade practice mixing military, paramilitary and civilian assets. Eastern waters are vital for wartime allied supplies.
Taiwanese defense officials told Reuters that China was "using law enforcement and scientific research as cover for harassment, seeking to expand their scope of operations during a non-conflict scenario to create an illusion of de facto jurisdiction." They said the steps undermine order and maritime rights. China's Taiwan Affairs Office and Ministry of National Defense did not respond.
The maritime militia dates to the 1950s and appears more often in the South China Sea. Analysts say it lets Beijing press claims while looking civilian. Two senior Taiwan officials confirmed the Minfudingyu, cutter 2502 and Xiang Yang Hong 03 were near Taiwan in mid-August. One official said the boat, in the People's Liberation Army maritime militia fleet, was operating "in coordination with Chinese coast guard maritime harassment drills." "The purpose of militia boats is to conduct substantive harassment," the official said. The other official said the three craft were operating "in an area not commonly used by Chinese vessels" and had been "designated for heightened monitoring."
An Apex plane found a Chinese group more than 30 nautical miles (34.5 miles) off Hualien, and the firm withheld the date over counter-reconnaissance concerns. Apex says the flights are independent yet fit the government's "whole of society resilience" initiative.
Honor Hung of Apex said warships, coast guard vessels, research ships and some civilian craft keep overlapping, "creating pressure in the waters surrounding Taiwan." The three ships sat across 10 nautical miles (11.5 miles). A light plane with a US-made radar can detect surface objects as small as 900 square centimeters (140 square inches), Reuters reported.

articles.title_orig: Flu season didn’t start when or where it was expected. Get your shot now, health officials say
articles.title_zh: Flu season didn’t start when or where it was expected. Get your shot now, health officials say
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
This year’s flu season started months early and in an unexpected part of the country, according to health officials.
The unusually early start to the season has prompted local health officials to urge people to get their flu shots as soon as possible.
In Los Angeles County, flu activity began rising in September, ahead of its typical early-November start, Dr. Dawn Terashita told The Times on Wednesday.
That isn’t a major surprise, said Terashita, associate director of the Los Angeles County Department of Public Health’s Acute Communicable Disease Control Program. Flu tends to be “very unpredictable,” she said, due to the ways that it mutates.
But another unusual factor was that the flu season started this year in the Western states.
Typically, the flu starts in the South and Southeast, Dr. Helen Chu of the University of Washington School of Medicine told Huffpost . The disease “then sort of migrates up and then west,” Chu said, so the West Coast tends to get the flu last.
Terashita said it’s too soon to know the reason behind this phenomenon.
The county’s flu season started on Sept. 28. But the early start alone, she said, isn’t an indicator that the season will be more severe, she said.
The rate at which flu tests are coming back positive since the season’s start has been high in the San Francisco Bay Area and moderate in Southern California and the Sacramento Valley. Flu hospital admission rates remain low across California. So far this year, there have been 34 flu-related deaths in the state, according to the state Department of Public Health’s online dashboard .
San Francisco confirmed its first flu death of the season last week . Los Angeles County has not logged any influenza deaths yet this season, Terashita said. In the 2025-26 flu season, the county recorded 126 influenza deaths, a relatively low total, she noted.
Health officials say vaccination is the best form of protection against the flu and are urging people to get their shots soon.
Dr. Peter Chin-Hong, a UC San Francisco infectious-disease expert, said people should aim to get the shot ideally before mid-October. For most, he said, the standard flu shot suffices, though he noted there are other options, including a nasal spray version — great for almost anyone with a fear of needles — and higher-dosage shots. The stronger shots have four times the antigen and are approved for those 65 and older.
The current variant, H3N2 subclade K, appears similar to last year’s strain and is included in this year’s vaccine, reducing concern about a major mismatch between the vaccine and the flu strain, Chin-Hong said.
“The ball is in our court because vaccination behavior drives how we tackle the flu,” he said. “This year we have less excuse because the flu vaccine is well-matched in general to ... what has been circulating so far.”
Los Angeles County’s most severe flu season in recent memory was the 2009 pandemic, according to Terashita. That year, the H1N1 virus led to a high number of hospitalizations and deaths around the world, The Times reported at the time.
Flu cases almost disappeared during the COVID-19 pandemic, Terashita said. As people resumed gatherings and eased up on measures including masking and social distancing, the county saw upticks in flu cases in 2024 and 2025.
“We’re just watching and waiting right now” to see how severe the flu season will be, she said, “but it is a good reminder to everyone that it’s a very good thing you can do to protect yourself, which is get the vaccine.”
Times staff writer Rong-Gong Lin contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Gruesome injuries throw spotlight on France’s policing of high school protests
articles.title_zh: Gruesome injuries throw spotlight on France’s policing of high school protests
articles.content_orig:
PARIS — The police tear gas grenade shattered the 14-year-old’s jaw and many of his teeth. The officer who fired it was taken into custody a week later and charged with violent mutilation, punishable by up to 15 years in prison. Following surgery, the boy cannot speak and can only eat with a straw, his mother says.
Other adolescents have also suffered life-changing injuries blamed on police weaponry during nationwide protests by high school students demanding more funding for run-down schools. In the former mining town of Lens, a 15-year-old lost a hand in an incident involving a police stun grenade. In Tours, in the wine-making Loire region, the prosecutor there says a police riot-control round is suspected in the partial blinding of a 16-year-old.
Beyond physical wounds, the massive use of police arrests and tactics that government critics and human rights campaigners allege have been unnecessarily violent is giving a generation of French schoolchildren — and soon-to-be voters — a real-life education about state power and their rights as citizens, and how the two sometimes clash.
“It politicizes you at an incredible speed,” said Alexis Baudelin, a Paris attorney for more than a dozen youngsters taken into custody.
“For many of them — for all of them — this was one of the first times that they’d taken part in a demonstration, coming together in a public space to voice demands they considered legitimate.”
Police have swept up thousands of young people
According to the Interior Ministry, police have made more than 6,600 arrests — mostly of people under 18 — since protests began snowballing last week, including 488 people detained during nationwide demonstrations Tuesday. The movement demanding increased funds and more replacement teachers for schools started in a Paris-region high school in mid-September.
Lawyers and researchers who study French policing caution that the muscular response could spawn disillusioned young adults soured on the Republic and its promises of “ Liberty, Equality, Fraternity. “Police have been less forgiving with teenage protesters than they previously were when farmers, a powerful lobby in France, doused government buildings with manure, blocked roads and set fires.
Baudelin, the lawyer, said his young clients have had a crash course in “unrestrained violence from the police.”
“Being locked up for hours and hours with nothing, in cells that are for the most part extremely unsanitary, in police stations that smell terrible, where you can’t sleep, with police officers telling you that if you don’t talk, if you don’t tell the truth, threatening you, telling you that your life is going to be ruined,” he said.
“It’s an experience that can be deeply traumatic and is completely out of proportion.”
Amid a growing outcry, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez announced Wednesday that the model of stun grenade suspected of mutilating the teenager in Lens will no longer be used against high schoolers, in light, he said, of a “strong possibility” that such a weapon was involved in ripping off the pupil’s hand.
“We need to understand exactly what happened,” Nunez said.
Still, he has also defended police actions as proportionate in “almost all cases.” He says police have been obliged to intervene when protests led to rioting, vandalism and other violence, and have done so mindful that they’re largely dealing with children.
“You don’t handle a high schoolers’ movement in the same way as one by adults,” the minister said to broadcaster RTL.
In the case of the 14-year-old with a smashed jaw and teeth, the officer who fired his grenade launcher directly at him during a protest in Saint-Ouen l’Aumone, northwest of Paris, said during questioning in custody that he acted in “a fraction of a second” to protect a female colleague who’d exchanged blows with the boy, according to a statement from the prosecutor’s office leading the investigation.
It described the officer’s actions as disproportionate, resulting in a preliminary charge against him of violence by a public official causing mutilation or permanent disability. Suspended from duty and barred from carrying a gun, he is the first officer facing potential prosecution in 18 investigations opened so far into suspected police misconduct during the protests.
The boy, Eden, sent his mother a video from outside his school, showing police and some protesters, just moments before the officer shot him with the gas grenade, she said, speaking to The Associated Press and other media on condition that she not be identified to preserve the anonymity of her child.
But when she then called him, it was one of his classmates who answered, screaming that her son had been hit in the face and was on the ground, bleeding with his jaw and top teeth broken and bottom teeth “completely ripped out,” she said.
“It’s shameful, it’s appalling, it’s violent, it’s disgusting, it’s despicable — I could give you a whole list of words,” she said. “They are dealing with children. And children demanding what? Simply better conditions in which to study.”
In the crowds that demonstrated in Paris on Tuesday, marching boisterously from one city square to another, AP found three Paris-region teenagers who said they were arrested, handcuffed, searched, held in custody but then released with no criminal charges last week.
Samy and Warkya, both 17, said they were detained together with another friend. They believe that police picked on them because of their color. Warkya and the other friend are Black and Samy described himself as Arab. French officials have repeatedly denied that there is racism in the police ranks. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said in parliament this week that such accusations are “lies.”
Samy said the officers who stopped them said, “’You, you and you, you’re coming with us.’” There was no apparent motive, because “we weren’t wearing hoodies, we had nothing on us, our faces were visible,” he said.
“Here in France, they don’t listen to us. They would rather send in the police than listen to us and put measures in place to improve our daily lives,” he said.
Warkya said her first experience of police custody only reinforced her determination to protest but also taught her to run when officers appear.
“The police are more powerful than us,” she said. “There’s nothing we can do.”

articles.title_orig: Texts Show Kimberly Guilfoyle Seeking $100,000 and Offering Access to Trump Officials
articles.title_zh: Texts Show Kimberly Guilfoyle Seeking $100,000 and Offering Access to Trump Officials
articles.content_orig:
Vice President JD Vance said Thursday he took issue with anyone seeking financial gain in exchange for access to Trump administration officials after a report claimed Kimberly Guilfoyle, the US ambassador to Greece, sought funds and offered access to top administration officials ahead of her confirmation.
“Obviously I don’t love that,” Vance said when a reporter asked whether he had any reaction to a scenario where an American ambassador tried to exchange access for funds. The reporter did not name Guilfoyle specifically.
The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday that Guilfoyle had asked a donor and former congressional candidate for $100,000 to pay off an American Express bill. CNN has reached out to Guilfoyle. A lawyer for the ambassador told the Journal that Guilfoyle disputed the authenticity of the messages.
Vance, who said he was unsure of the specifics of the episode, reserved further comment during a press conference on visa fraud.
But the vice president said in general he was uncomfortable with access-for-pay schemes.
“Of course I don’t like anybody selling access to another government official, certainly a high-level government official,” he said.
“But you know, I assume you’re talking about a specific case, and I can’t say with confidence that the case you’re talking about is actually reflective of of the way you’re describing it,” he added.
According to the Journal, the donor, Eric Deters, had been seeking Guilfoyle’s help in “getting the attention of the new Trump administration on some personal tax and legal issues.”
“Honey please I need you to get this done for me today,” Guilfoyle texted Deters days ahead of her confirmation hearing, according to the Journal. Deters didn’t make the payment, the newspaper reported.
This is a developing story and will be updated.

articles.title_orig: Comebacks for wild tigers, tuna and sea turtles prove nature loss can be reversed, scientists say
articles.title_zh: Comebacks for wild tigers, tuna and sea turtles prove nature loss can be reversed, scientists say
articles.content_orig:
A landmark report reveals that the world must change the way it produces food to avoid a biodiversity collapse
Conservation comebacks for wild tigers, tuna and green​ sea turtles prove that global nature loss can be reversed, ​scientists have said. ​But a report warns food production must be the next ​“positive tipping point​” if the world is to avert biodiversity collapse.
The World Wildlife Fund ( WWF ) analysed nearly 36,000 animal populations and more than 5,000 species, producing the largest ever database of vertebrate wildlife. Scientists found populations had declined by an average of 73% since 1970, showing that “nature continues to be degraded at an alarming scale”, with “no sign of losses slowing”.
Nature loss is no longer just an environmental challenge but a direct threat to the global economy, the report says, noting that about half of global GDP – roughly $58tn (£44tn) in 2023 – depends on nature and its ecosystem services. The authors write that species collapse now poses an “existential threat to economic stability, geopolitical security and human wellbeing”.
Animal populations were found to be falling most sharply in tropical, biodiversity-rich regions, while trends in northern temperate parts of the world appeared much gentler.
In Latin America and the Caribbean, land and freshwater wildlife populations fell by an average of 95% between 1970 and 2022, while the equivalent declines were 80% in Africa and 23% in Europe and Central Asia.
Freshwater wildlife suffered the sharpest losses across the world’s ecosystems, with monitored populations in rivers and lakes down by an average of 85%, compared with 69% for land species and 59% for marine species.
Tanya Steele, the chief executive of WWF UK, said: “Nature loss is not just a crisis for wildlife. It’s already sending us the bill through growing risks to our food security, water supplies, economy and resilience to climate shocks.
“We stand at a fork in the road: either we continue paying the rising price of nature loss, or we invest in nature’s recovery and a future where people and wildlife can thrive together.”
But despite the pattern of global biodiversity decline, wild tigers, green sea turtles and bluefin tuna are recovering, the report said, showing that “it is still possible to reverse the global loss of nature when action is taken”.
In 2010, about 3,200 wild tigers remained globally and the species was sliding toward extinction. After sustained and targeted conservation interventions, the population has grown to roughly 5,700, an increase of more than 70%.
Becci May, WWF UK’s tiger lead, said the remarkable comeback of wild tigers demonstrated the “science of hope” and proved that when climate and ecological action was taken, change was possible.
The report said Atlantic and Pacific bluefin tuna populations, which were collapsing after decades of overfishing, had now recovered to the point where neither was now considered threatened.
Last year, the green sea turtle became the first marine turtle ever downlisted from endangered to “least concern” on the IUCN red list, reflecting 50 years of coordinated conservation work across about 80 countries.
Dr Mike Barrett, the chief scientific adviser for WWF UK and a co-author of the report, said: “These are examples that show that nature can recover even when pushed right to the brink, and they provide us with inspiration. It’s also very clear that conservation alone cannot tackle the scale of threats facing nature.”
He said nature would have no chance of recovery if “negative tipping points ” – self-reinforcing, irreversible ecological changes that accelerate climate crisis – were passed. “The systems which drive nature’s loss have to be transformed. And that’s energy, food and finance,” he said.
“Our report shows that we’ve already passed the tipping point in the energy sector with the take-up of renewable energy . That transition is now unstoppable. It’s not happening fast enough, but it is unstoppable.”
Humanity must likewise adapt the way it produces food, he said. “Agriculture is the single largest cause of habitat loss and degradation and therefore the loss of biodiversity. It’s also a major source of greenhouse gas emissions and so helps drive climate change, so you have that feedback.”
Dr Steve Smith, a research fellow from the University of Exeter and a co-author of the report, said: “The biggest prize for nature recovery would be a sustainable and healthy food system, but it’s currently the farthest away from positively tipping. For example, agricultural expansion drives almost 90% of deforestation worldwide.”
Positive tipping points are thresholds beyond which a sustainable technology or practice becomes increasingly cheap, widespread or politically popular, allowing progress to become self-propelling.

articles.title_orig: A hurricane could cripple US refining when the world can least afford it
articles.title_zh: A hurricane could cripple US refining when the world can least afford it
articles.content_orig:
The global energy system is already being pushed to the brink. A hurricane barreling down on America’s refining nerve center is the last thing that’s needed.
Isaias, the Atlantic season’s first hurricane , is arriving at a time when there is almost no margin for error.
US refineries, mostly located along the Gulf Coast, are running as hard as they can to offset war-driven outages overseas. Fuel inventories that act as shock absorbers have already been tapped. And America’s emergency oil stockpile is at the lowest level since 1982.
Hurricane Isaias “could be a gigantic event. It’s the worst time something like this could happen in 25 years,” said Robert Yawger, director of energy futures at Mizuho Securities.
The actual impact of Isaias will depend on the storm’s path and intensity.
Current forecasts call for the storm to hit east of New Orleans, a major refining hub, which should spare vital energy infrastructure from the storm’s worst.
Still, major oil producers including Shell, Chevron and BP have evacuated non-essential personnel from oil platforms in the Gulf and curtailed production .
As of midday Wednesday, about 512,000 barrels per day of Gulf of Mexico oil production had been shut in, according to the federal agency Marine Minerals Administration.
That amounts to about 25% of the region’s production. And about 16% of current natural gas production in the Gulf of Mexico has been sidelined.
The risk is that the storm’s damage could squeeze supply chains even more, further raising historically high prices.
The Iran war, combined with Ukrainian drone attacks in Russia and export restrictions in China, have catapulted diesel prices to all-time highs. Gasoline was more than $4.40 per gallon last week and has never been this expensive at this time of year.
How gas station owners set their prices
About 2.7 million barrels per day, or 14%, of America’s refining capacity, lie within or near the projected of the path of the storm, according to Andy Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates.
Lipow said he expects at least some refineries in the New Orleans/Baton Rouge and Mississippi/Alabama regions will have to slow down how much oil they turn into gasoline, diesel and jet fuel.
Tankers delivering oil to refineries and loading fuel out of refineries could get delayed as well. This would particularly impact Florida because the state relies on shipments of fuel from the Gulf Coast.
“There is no slack in the system to make up for lost refinery capacity. Lost production will have to come out of already low commercial inventories,” Lipow wrote in an email.
Those commercial inventories have been whittled away.
Gasoline stockpiles recently fell to their lowest seasonal record since 2012, according to federal data.
Distillate inventories, which include mostly diesel, are at their lowest level for early October since tracking started in the early 1980s.
Not only that, but the Strategic Petroleum Reserve has been aggressively drained to ease the energy shock. The SPR now holds about 283 million barrels of crude, the least since 1982 when the emergency reserve was being filled during the Reagan administration.
Refineries in the Middle East have been damaged by the Iran war, or have struggled to get shipments out to the rest of the world. Refineries in Russia have been destroyed or damaged by drone attacks. And China, seeking to avoid fuel shortages, has restricted its exports.
US refineries, operating at about 95% of their capacity, are one of the remaining key sources for the global fuel supply.
“It would be a disaster if US refining capacity has to come off the market. It would basically force a diesel export ban,” said Yawger, the Mizuho executive, who added that he is not in favor of restricting US diesel exports .
Much depends on the intensity of the storm, including the severity of flooding and wind damage. Isaias could peak as a Category 2 storm with 110 mph winds by early Friday, but is expected to weaken somewhat before landfall.
Even with a Category 1 hurricane, it can take a week to return refining operations to normal.

articles.title_orig: What impact Old Vine Seal can have on world’s oldest vineyards
articles.title_zh: What impact Old Vine Seal can have on world’s oldest vineyards
articles.content_orig:
What started way back in 2010 as a grassroots, volunteer effort by wine critic Jancis Robinson MW and her team to record all the vineyards in the world that qualify as old vines has developed into the full blown Old Vine Registry that now includes close to 5,000 producers. It has now introduced the OV Seal to give those producers the chance to promote, on their label, how old their vines are and help spread the word to wine drinkers about the importance and significance of old vines. Alder Yarrow, architect and manager of the OVR explains what he hopes the new seal can achieve.
Tell us about the new seal initiative you have introduced?
The creation and growth of the Old Vine Registry has always been predicated on the idea that we can’t preserve or value what we don’t know about. So our first and ongoing goal has been to catalogue old vine vineyards everywhere.
In addition to knowing they exist, however, to keep them in the ground we have to make sure they remain economically sustainable for those who farm them, and one of the ways to do this is to drive increased awareness and sales of the wines that get made from old vineyards.
In order to do that, the Old Vine Registry had to get out of the internet and into the real world, and the OVR Seal is our attempt to do that—to start having the conversation about old vines at the shelf level.
What do you hope to achieve with it that you can’t currently do with the Registry?
The Old Vine Registery now has the records of nearly 5,000 producers in its database
By allowing registered producers to put the OVR Seal on their bottles, we are giving wineries around the world the chance to declare how old their vineyards are and to give interested consumers a destination to learn more, in the form of the Old Vine Registry listing for their vineyard.
This offers an opportunity for consumers to learn and engage in a way that the use of words such as “vieilles vignes” or “old vines” don’t offer. Also unlike those terms, which mostly have no legal meaning or regulation guiding their usage around the world, the OVR Seal offers a more concrete and legitimate declaration that a vineyard truly is old.
What do producers or winemakers need to do in order to use the seal?
In order to use the seal, producers must have their vineyard(s) listed in the Old Vine Registry, which is free and easy to do. Once that has occurred, a producer must simply pay a one-time fee of $300 to get access to seal artwork that corresponds to the age of their registered vines.
They are then free to use the seal on their packaging and digital marketing materials associated with wines made from their registered vineyard.
You are launching the seal with a few initial producers - who are they and why have they come on first?
We teased the fact that the Seal was coming back in June, and a number of wineries immediately reached out asking how they might get access to the seal. We offered the opportunity to get early access to the seal to all the producers who made such inquiries, and eleven of them stepped up and said they wanted to particpate.
Derek Mossman Knapp of Chile's Garage Wine Company is one of the first producers to take on the Old Vine Registery seal
Our launch partners are: Seghesio Family Vineyards and Bedrock Wine Company in Sonoma, Garage Wine Company in Chile, Versado and Ciclo Andino in Mendoza, AYA Estate in Bulgaria, Sown Estate in Napa, Woldridge Creek Winery in Oregon, Methymnaeos Organic Vineyards in Greece, Plaimont in Gascony, and Tenuta Santa Maria in Soave.
These are all wineries that have, at a minimum, made commitments to making old vineyards a key part of their philosophical approach to winemaking. Some of them, like Bedrock Wine Company or Garage Wine Company, go much further than that, as shepherds of some of the world’s oldest and most storied vineyards.
How will producers be able to use it in their marketing and on their labels?
The seal is available for use in the context of products and marketing that are specific to one or more vineyards that are recorded in the Old Vine Registry. The age-specific seal can be used on wine packaging if 85% of the grapes come from one or more registered vineyards that are at least as old as the age-mark on the seal. In the same fashion, the seal may also be used on technical sheets or sell-sheets or even e-commerce product pages for specific individual wines.
We also anticipate producers using the seal in the context of marketing a specific registered vineyard, perhaps on websites or in print marketing, or even by putting a sign in the vineyard itself. We’re really open to however wineries want to use the seal, provided it is always in the context of mentioning or referencing a specific vineyard rather than generic marketing about the brand as a whole.
What percentage of producers who are in the registry do you hope to sign up to use the seal?
Examples of how producers are using the Old Vine Registry seal on their labels
We honestly have no idea how many wineries are going to be excited about this seal. Many producers don’t even know that their vineyards are listed in the Old Vine Registry. Of the 5,474 unique producers listed in the Old Vine Registry, if we got 10% of them using the seal, I would consider that a smashing success.
Is there a registration cost to use the seal?
Yes, we’ve settled on a one-time $300 registration cost to use the seal. This amount was chosen to be affordable to even the smallest producers, while making sure that everyone who registers has at least a little skin in the game. The fee is not a recurring subscription, and registered producers are free to use the seal providing they have a qualified, registered vineyard that is still in the ground.
For those that don’t know the Old Vine Registry - what are your primary objectives?
As a registered nonprofit, Old Vine Registry exists to catalog the world’s vineyards over 35 years-old. Once recorded, we hope to drive awareness of and an increased appreciation for the value of old vineyards with the hopes that this leads to increased sales of the wines they produce, and ultimately their preservation.
How do you hope the seal will help your overall work?
The seal will hopefully become a point of difference and an opportunity for conversation between producers and their customers that brings the idea of old vines and what makes them special into the spotlight. If using the seal can get some of wine lovers to be more curious about old vines and why they matter we’re on our way to the ultimate outcome, which would be to create a legitimate commercial category for old vine wines.
We’re working towards a day when every serious wine list, every retailer, importer, and distributor, should have an old-vine section that is used to highlight the incredible wines made from the world’s old vineyards.
What other initiatives do you have planned for the OVR?
Alder Yarrow is manager of the Old Vine Registry - a role he is prepared to do on a voluntary basis
Once the OVR Seal program is up and running smoothly, we’re going to go back to making improvements to the Old Vine Registry website that will make it an even more valuable resource for the industry and academia. This will include publishing analysis on the increasingly sizeable set of data that the registry collects and different ways of interrogating that data.
And of course, we’re going to continue adding more and more vineyards to the registry. We’re not anywhere close to having even a quarter of the world’s old vineyards catalogued.
In October of 2024, the OIV published Resolution OIV-VITI 703-2024 which for the first time established an official definition of what “old vines” means for European wine. More importantly that resolution recommended "the cataloguing of old vineyards and old grapevines" and "to make openly available official data from the vineyard register to draw up vineyard maps and ascertain the age of vineyards.”

articles.title_orig: ‘Nature can recover’: Inside the race to rescue world’s crisis-hit wildlife
articles.title_zh: ‘Nature can recover’: Inside the race to rescue world’s crisis-hit wildlife
articles.content_orig:
Beneath the dense forest canopy of Uganda’s Bwindi Impenetrable National Park, a troop of gorillas is being quietly observed by a group of tourists who have each paid $800 for the privilege of the experience.
In villages around the park, a thriving economy has grown off the back of the gorillas’ presence here, from the sale of wood carvings to visitors and the provision of accommodation for up to 40,000 tourists a year.
In the national park, which sprawls along the edge of the Rift Valley and the border with the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), there are many local jobs for rangers and guides.
But deeper into the forest, more mountain gorillas live away from human contact, quietly enhancing the natural world around them through their daily routines of foraging, nest building and dispersing seeds.
And, crucially, by increasing their own populations.
In the 1980s, the mountain gorilla was on the fast track to extinction. Now, there are more than 1,100 living in thriving populations in Uganda, Rwanda and the DRC.
Theirs is a story of conservation success that spills beyond the species themselves, into the nature they live in, and the human communities they exist alongside.
“The mountain gorilla story shows us that conservation can work,” Tara Stoinski of the Dian Fossey Gorilla Fund tells Al Jazeera. “It’s a really important example of the effort that’s needed to make that happen – decades of sustained conservation action that includes direct protection, science-informed management and meaningful community support and involvement.”
This is welcome news for a natural world beset by crisis.
According to this year’s Living Planet Report by the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF), over the past 52 years, there has been a 73 percent decline in the average size of monitored wildlife populations. Across the world, habitats have been degraded and lost as overexploitation, climate change, pollution and invasive species take their toll.
But the report also highlights important recoveries in populations of green turtles, bluefin tuna, tigers and Southern African elephants. “For too long nature has been undervalued,” says Andrew Terry, chief conservation officer at the Zoological Society of London, who helped produce the report. “But these declines are not inevitable and change is possible. Nature can recover, and these stories are a powerful reminder of this.”
The WWF says these conservation successes demonstrate how international partnerships drive results. Intergovernmental commitments from tiger range countries, including India, Bhutan, Nepal, Laos and China, helped increase global wild tiger numbers by more than 70 percent between 2010 and 2025.
In 2025, the green sea turtle became the first marine turtle ever to be downlisted from “endangered” to “least concern” on the International Union for the Conservation of Nature Red List. That reflected 50 years of species research, active protection of nesting females and eggs, measures to reduce fishing gear and sustained community engagement.
Professor Brendon Godley is a leading conservation scientist at the University of Exeter and the Sharjah Marine Research Centre in the United Arab Emirates and has spent much of his career dedicated to researching and protecting sea turtles. “Conservation success stories are hugely important because they demonstrate that declines are not inevitable,” he tells Al Jazeera.
“The recovery of species such as green turtles shows that when science, policy, enforcement and public support align, populations can rebound, sometimes remarkably so. However, they are not grounds for complacency.”
Indeed, these conservation triumphs are small battles won in an ongoing war against the degradation of nature. The WWF’s Living Planet Report highlights the three systems that are primarily driving the destruction of nature: the global food system, which is the leading cause of habitat loss as areas are cleared to grow crops; the energy system, which fuels climate change through burning fossil fuels; and the finance system, which bankrolls harmful activities, for example, large-scale infrastructure or mining projects.
Kirsten Schuijt, director general of WWF, says these industries and systems need to be transformed. “Progress is already under way,” she tells Al Jazeera. “Not everywhere, and not yet at the scale required, but enough to demonstrate that change is possible.”
The return of a species can have a powerful effect. In 2010, Atlantic bluefin tuna populations had declined by 80 percent and the species was listed as endangered. They had disappeared from much of their historical range, including UK waters. Yet today they are returning in numbers not witnessed in generations, perhaps ever.
“What makes this story particularly powerful is that the recovery is visible,” says Tom Horton, research fellow at the University of Exeter. “Coastal communities, fishers and sea-users who had never seen a bluefin tuna in British waters are now encountering them regularly. It transforms conservation from an abstract concept into something tangible.”
These successes serve as inspiration for other conservation projects in the fight against species decline, like that of the largest primate on Earth, the critically endangered Grauer’s Gorilla. Its home range lies within the vast remote forests of the DRC, living in a landscape beset by instability and habitat loss. Its numbers have dropped by an estimated 60 percent to just 6,800 today.
Urbain Ngobobo, country director for the Dian Fossey Fund in the DRC, explains that the challenge of restoring numbers there is significant but so is the opportunity.
“Every forest we help communities protect,” he says, “every gorilla we are able to monitor and every young Congolese person who develops the skills to become a conservation leader, represents progress.
“That is where hope comes from – not from assuming the future will be easy, but from knowing that our actions today can change what is possible tomorrow.”

articles.title_orig: Oil prices rise sharply on Middle East tensions and US hurricane threat
articles.title_zh: Oil prices rise sharply on Middle East tensions and US hurricane threat
articles.content_orig:
Global bond market sell-off continues and stocks fall amid another wave of potential strikes against Iran
Business live – latest updates
Oil prices have risen sharply amid fears about escalating tensions in the Middle East and a squeeze on production from the threat of a hurricane off the US coast.
Brent crude, the international benchmark, rose by 3.8% to $104 a barrel on Thursday, triggering a wave of selling in the global bond and stock markets.
The White House has asked the Pentagon to draw up options for strikes against Iran before the US midterm elections, according to a report in The Atlantic. The report cited unnamed officials in Donald Trump’s administration who said the size and targets of potential strikes, and whether they will go ahead, are still being debated.
The report has weakened hopes that Trump will refrain from escalating the conflict with Iran before the midterm polls next month. A “limited operation” could be followed up by more substantial action after the midterms, it states.
Another wave of strikes against Iran represents further risk to oil supply from the Middle East, with the US-Israeli war against Tehran now entering its eighth month. Attacks on tankers in the strait of Hormuz reached their highest levels of ⁠the war, ⁠cutting ​traffic through the waterway and deepening fears about supply.
The latest attack came ⁠on Wednesday, when a tanker was hit by multiple projectiles off the north coast of Qatar , causing casualties, according to ​the United Kingdom Maritime ‌Trade Operations.
Oil prices also rose in response to a squeeze on production in the Gulf of Mexico, after the tropical storm Isaias strengthened to become the first hurricane of the Atlantic season.
Shell and Chevron both said they were shutting down production as the storm approached the region, forecast to make landfall on Friday or Saturday.
Maersk, the Danish shipping group, added to worries around rising energy prices on Thursday after it said it was increasing its emergency fuel surcharge on all its export collections and import deliveries. The rise in energy prices has fed fears about inflation, reinforcing expectations that central banks will have to raise their interest rates in order to control rising prices.
A sell-off in global bond markets continued on Thursday.
In the UK, the yield on the 30-year gilt – the benchmark for the cost of long-term government borrowing – rose by 3 basis points to 6.0117%, after touching 6.036% on Wednesday, the highest since January 1998.
The 10-year gilt yield rose by 5 basis points to 5.48%, approaching the 5.5% mark, returning to levels not seen since July 2007.
after newsletter promotion
In France, which has been hit particularly hard over worries around its rising debt and growing spending , the 10-year yield rose by 6 basis points to 4.931%, just behind the 24-year high of 4.994% it hit last week. Yields rise when prices fall.
The German 10-year yield, the benchmark for European debt, rose by 2 basis points to 3.504%.
The yield on the US 10-year treasury, which is widely considered the best quality government debt on the market, rose by 5 basis points to 5.331%.
Global stocks also fell, with Japan’s Nikkei share index falling 1.4% and the South Korean Kospi down 2.6%.
In Europe, the Stoxx Europe 600, which tracks the biggest companies on the continent, dropped 0.9%. The UK’s FTSE 100 slipped by 0.4% in early trading on Thursday.
