articles.title_orig: Trump considers ‘terminating’ campaign advisers after Balkans trip
articles.title_zh: Trump considers ‘terminating’ campaign advisers after Balkans trip
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump on Wednesday distanced himself from two of his top political advisers — less than 30 days before the midterm elections — writing that if their outside work presents a conflict, “I will terminate them, immediately!”
Trump’s warning came after The New York Times published a report detailing how James Blair, one of the president’s former deputy chiefs of staff who now leads his outside political operation, and Chris LaCivita, Trump’s 2024 co-campaign manager, traveled to the Balkans last week for paid work on behalf of a pro-Russian government.
Trump was unaware that the two men had traveled to the Balkans – or that the pro-Russian government was among their clientele – until he was briefed on the impending New York Times piece, sources familiar with the situation told CNN. The president then made a series of phone calls Tuesday night asking his allies what their take on the story was, the sources said.
One source said Trump appeared annoyed, and another veteran Republican who is in touch with the president told CNN that Trump was “pissed” by the report – particularly at the revelation that the two advisers had been abroad in the home stretch of the midterm campaign, profiting off their association with him.
“Tone deaf,” the veteran Republican said of the advisers’ conduct.
But another source said Trump was simply seeking a range of opinions on what had been reported.
Trump – who has been actively campaigning for Republicans ahead of November’s midterms – ultimately decided he wanted to respond to the story, two of the sources told CNN. So on Wednesday, one of the sources said, he dictated a Truth Social post to aide Natalie Harp while in the Oval Office, commenting to those in the room that both Blair and LaCivita are outside consultants and are allowed to have other clients. One source said that at that moment, he did not seem irked.
“Chris LaCivita and James Blair are outside consultants. They do not work for me, other than as outside consultants. They most likely have numerous clients, but for that, you would have to ask them,” Trump posted.
“I do not have any idea who else they work for but will, on reflection, ask them and, if there’s a conflict, I will terminate them, immediately!” Trump wrote.
The president continued distancing himself from the two advisers and downplayed any conflict of interest later Wednesday. “They don’t have a conflict because they’re independent people,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office.
“I assume they have a lot of clients,” he went on. “So I don’t know their contract. If I thought they had a conflict … I would terminate.”
He also noted that neither currently works in the White House.
“Well they’re allowed to do that,” Trump told CNN. “They have a lot of clients and it’s okay. I’m a client over there, they have a consulting firm I guess, separately, as all people in Washington do. That’s pretty common.”
According to the Times, Blair and LaCivita traveled to Republika Srpska, a territory in Bosnia and Herzegovina, ahead of elections there on Sunday. The trip came as polls show Republicans are facing severe electoral challenges in the United States.
Blair and LaCivita “were paid hundreds of thousands of dollars each through a Washington-based law firm that was retained by Republika Srpska’s government to provide counsel on voting issues,” the Times reported.
They said the work was for the government and not the nationalist party that controls it, though they are essentially one and the same.
Blair currently leads Trump’s super PAC, MAGA Inc., and has been tasked with heading up the president’s midterm elections strategy. LaCivita is a senior adviser at MAGA Inc.
The group has been spending tens of millions of dollars trying to bolster Republican candidates ahead of the midterms, including some in reliably red territory who now appear vulnerable.
This story has been updated with additional developments.
CNN’s Kevin Liptak contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Hispanic Heritage Month: Israel Balderas helps students find their passion in a world ‘out of control’
articles.title_zh: Hispanic Heritage Month: Israel Balderas helps students find their passion in a world ‘out of control’
articles.content_orig:
A self-described “Texan American with a Mexican heart,” Assistant Professor of Journalism Israel Balderas says at the center of his sense of belonging at Elon are his students.
Israel Balderas is no stranger to the public eye. The First Amendment attorney and former television journalist regularly speaks with media outlets about current events, an extension of the work he does as an assistant professor of journalism at Elon University.
“As an academic, my relationship is going out in the name of Elon, even though I speak for myself,” said Balderas. “I’m always saying, ‘Here at Elon, we don’t make small plans. We’re always thinking bigger, and because we are a national school, what would help us to continue to be a national school?’ To me, my responsibility as an academic is to get my name out there.”
For Balderas, that work is closely connected to the sense of belonging he has found at Elon and the university’s teacher-scholar-mentor model. At the center of it all are his students.
“When my students leave, and the class is over, I say, ‘Love you. Mean it.’ And we throw the word love around a lot,” Balderas said. “But, to me, as a teacher, I think love from a teacher to a student is this idea, and it’s my ‘why.’ My ‘why’ is that I’m passionate about teaching students how to find their passion in a world that is out of control.”
Balderas began his journalism career as a freelance reporter and producer for several outlets in Washington, D.C. His coverage of the 2000 presidential election helped spur an interest in legal studies, as did a friendly competition with his sister over who could earn the higher score on the LSAT.
Growing up in a single-parent Hispanic household, Balderas said education was “non-negotiable.” He went on to earn his Juris Doctor from the Catholic University of America while working as a producer at FOX News Channel.
In the years that followed, Balderas worked for television stations across Florida, North Carolina and Texas. His work earned multiple industry accolades, including an Emmy for Best Continuing Coverage and recognition from the Radio Television Digital News Association of the Carolinas as best TV news anchor.
My ‘why’ is that I’m passionate about teaching students how to find their passion in a world that is out of control.
-Israel Balderas, assistant professor of journalism
Alongside his journalism career, Balderas took on legal work for the Center for Human Rights and Constitutional Law, We The Action and the Society of Professional Journalists. His pro bono work included representing migrant children at the U.S.-Mexico border and helping nonprofits navigate financial aid during the COVID-19 pandemic.
In 2017, Balderas left television news to spend more time with his family and transitioned to higher education, first teaching at a university in West Palm Beach, Florida, before joining Elon’s faculty in 2021.
“I love the mission of Elon University,” Balderas said. “The mission of Elon is that it ‘embraces its founder’s vision of an academic community that transforms mind, body, and spirit and encourages freedom of thought and liberty of conscience.’ And I said during my interview, that’s what a First Amendment professor teaches. That’s it.”
Journalism major Lily Molina ’27 took Balderas’ Media Law & Ethics course and says having a Latino professor in the journalism department made her feel welcomed as an aspiring Latina journalist.
“ I am really passionate about covering stories centered around my community, and Balderas has supported me in doing that. It’s comforting to have someone who I can speak Spanish to and not feel judged,” she said. “This is just one of the reasons why having diversity within departments is so important.”
A self-described “Texan American with a Mexican heart,” Balderas views Hispanic Heritage Month through the lens of the cultures that have shaped the United States.
“It’s about celebrating many cultures who have been able to adapt their cultures to this idea of ‘American citizen,’” he said. “What I love about Hispanic Heritage Month is that we get to show off the beauty of our diversity in a society that is diverse.”
Balderas describes that blending of cultures as a “stew,” one he sees reflected regularly on Elon’s campus. He points to El Centro, a space within the Center for Race, Ethnicity and Diversity Education that celebrates Latine and Hispanic cultures while sharing them with the broader Elon community.
“Every time I go to El Centro, there are kids from all over, and they’re all happy, and they’re ready to tell us about their abuelita (grandmother), they’re ready to tell us about their family,” Balderas said. “They’re ready to tell us about the history of their country. And in sharing all that, we get to build community together.”
As part of Hispanic Heritage Month, Elon University is sharing stories that celebrate the contributions, identities and experiences of students, faculty and staff. This month recognizes the rich histories and cultures of Hispanic and Latine communities, while also honoring the ways these traditions connect with and inspire people of all backgrounds. This month provides a special opportunity to honor Hispanic and Latine heritage, but it also serves as an invitation for all members of the university to engage, learn and celebrate together.

articles.title_orig: World of Warcraft: Forever- The Future of Skyborne Visual Updates
articles.title_zh: World of Warcraft: Forever- The Future of Skyborne Visual Updates
articles.content_orig:
The World of Warcraft development team began our journey into World of Warcraft: Forever with ambitions that grew and evolved over time. Our aim has always been to uphold the original WoW era aesthetic, while giving players more choice in how they experience Azeroth.
Over the course of development, we have been aligning on the right range of fidelity and what feels like it belongs in the WoW: Forever world and what does not. The team has learned much in the process, and that will continue to strengthen more with future content.
Along the way, there were some ideas the team wanted to explore that ultimately didn’t quite meet the consistency and cohesion we are aiming for. To align with our goals better, we are taking aim at updating some of those visuals for the future. Here is one example of how we are revisiting the High Definition (HD) Skyborne Druid forms.
We removed a bit of the softness, added more detailed fur textures, and adjusted the color saturation. The Skyborne are from an exotic environment, and their Druid forms reflect that, but we don't want that to be dissonant with the visual language of other creatures in the world.
In choosing to offer an SD or HD toggle for player characters, we focused on the pre-existing races from original World of Warcraft since many people have an attachment to those models. However, we have heard feedback that the HD Skyborne can be jarring by contrast when placed in the same world as the SD models and world, and we agree.
So, for those of us that prefer the look of SD models and want more choice, Skyborne player characters (and yes SD Druid forms) are in development and arriving early 2027. We look forward to sharing more information closer to that date. For now, here is an early work in progress image.
This is just the start of our journey, and the whole team is thrilled with the reception for World of Warcraft: Forever . As we continue refining this vision together, we look forward to what lies ahead—for the Horde! For the Alliance! Forever!

articles.title_orig: China’s AI startups can match the U.S.’s models. They can’t yet match the U.S.’s money
articles.title_zh: China’s AI startups can match the U.S.’s models. They can’t yet match the U.S.’s money
articles.content_orig:
Alvin Yap is the chief executive officer for Asia at EquitiesFirst
By many measures, China is fast catching up with the U.S. in AI development. Moonshot’s Kimi K3—the world’s largest open-weight model—has approached the performance of America’s frontier systems. Analysts estimate the best Chinese models are now just four months behind the most sophisticated releases from OpenAI and Anthropic, compared to seven months at the start of the year.
Chinese models have gone from 1.2% of token traffic (a common way to calculate AI usage) in 2024 to more than half of the total by the summer of 2026.
But the biggest threat to that next wave is not technology. It’s money. Between 2023 and 2026, venture funding into U.S. AI companies topped $380 billion; China’s start-ups received barely a tenth of that figure, according to Boston Consulting Group.
In the past, Chinese entrepreneurs looked to state guidance funds and venture capital backing, but policy-driven funds are known to prioritize later-stage startups while early-stage venture capital is only just recovering from a three-year fundraising drought .
There are three reasons why broader funding channels should be a priority for entrepreneurs in the AI economy.
First, inflation is taking hold inside the AI economy. CXMT, for example, has been raising memory prices for months and held firm even when Huawei, one of its largest customers, demanded relief .
The war for AI talent is just as fierce: postings for AI-related roles surged roughly twelvefold year-on-year in early 2026. Algorithm engineers specializing in large language models command some of the highest pay packages of any technical role in China.
Founders must also outcompete deep-pocketed former employers and U.S. rivals. More than half of studies presented at the world’s top AI conference had lead authors based in China. China’s AI talent is known to be in demand worldwide.
Second, external funding is scarce. Venture investment in China totaled just $20 billion in the first quarter of 2026, against $267 billion in the U.S. China has raised impressive sums this year—assets under management for newly registered VC funds hit 154 billion yuan ($22.8 billion) in the first five monthes, already exceeding last year’s total—but that is still far below what US venture capital regularly deploys.
Meanwhile, China’s state banks, although directed to prioritize technology lending, are absorbing rising non-performing loans elsewhere on their books, which could lead to weaker overall credit supply.
Third, profitability will take a while to achieve. Chinese enterprise software firms primarily sell into the domestic market , which limits their revenue base. U.S. rivals have a head start: a global customer base, stronger brand recognition, and R&D budgets deep enough to fund everything from enterprise-grade cybersecurity to polished customer experience design.
To be sure, the next generation of AI ventures may not need vast amounts of capital to build applications on top of existing models or fill the gaps in the tech value chain.  Enterprise customers can also provide essential development funding.
Entrepreneurs must nevertheless cope without the kind of financial support that is available for the AI sector in the U.S. Closing the performance gap increasingly depends on bulking up in-house computing capacity—yet China’s AI infrastructure spending remains a fraction of what is being spent in the U.S.
This is where access to Hong Kong’s finance industry will play a growing role. Its capital markets remain one of the few channels still capable of moving global capital toward Chinese enterprise at scale. More than 430 applicants are in the IPO pipeline in the second half of 2026.
The IPO pipeline, however, tells its own story. Many Chinese technology startups are choosing to list earlier than the previous generation of companies did because they lack an alternative.
Compare that with the U.S., where the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic have grown to an enormous scale by raising private capital. OpenAI closed a round of more than $100 billion earlier this year, while Anthropic raised $65 billion in May. China’s leading model developers, Zhipu AI and MiniMax, beat OpenAI and Anthropic to the public markets—but their Hong Kong IPOs in January raised just $558 million and $620 million respectively, despite heavy over-subscription.
Private credit is another route. Asia-Pacific private credit assets are projected to grow from $59 billion in 2024 to $92 billion by 2027, with China accounting for a fifth of the region’s activity . However, these loan providers tend to prioritize bigger or established companies.
It is already clear that the AI sector, unlike the software sector, will not be dominated by U.S. firms alone. China’s startups have learned the lessons of the previous decade, commanding global respect and winning a growing customer base. The country’s open-weight strategy has given its leading AI companies a cost advantage – even Silicon Valley leaders acknowledge it.
For China’s latest generation of AI entrepreneurs, venture capital and bank loans—the two main sources of start-up funding – may not be enough in the coming years. Keeping pace in the AI race will require using every asset and every channel available. It may mean a public listing earlier than they would have preferred, exploring the growing private credit ecosystem, revenue sharing with customers or leveraging the equity they hold as collateral.
The entrepreneurs involved in the next wave of China’s AI development will need to be creative with funding to maintain their competitive edge at a time when overseas rivals are spending 10 times as much.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Dow Opens Lower, Treasury Yields Hit Fresh 24-Year Highs — Live Updates
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Dow Opens Lower, Treasury Yields Hit Fresh 24-Year Highs — Live Updates
articles.content_orig:
U.S. Treasury yields came off their highs after a solid sale of 10-year notes. Earlier, the 10-year yield rose to its highest level in more than two decades.
The 10-year Treasury last traded more than 1 basis point higher at 5.286%. Earlier in the session, it reached 5.35%, its highest level since 2002. The 30-year Treasury bond yield also traded below a 24-year high, at 5.666%.
One basis point equals 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
The Treasury sold $39 billion of 10-year notes in an auction on Wednesday. According to BMO, the sale was "strong", with higher than average bidding from non-dealers.
Indirect bidders, which include global central banks, took 80.3% of the auction — above a 10-auction average of 72.4%. Direct bidders, scooped up 17.1% of the sale, just below an average of 18.3%. Dealers, meanwhile, bought just 2.5% of the notes offered, well below a 9.4% mean.
"The 24-year highs in rates brought out the buyers and resulted in a great auction," said Peter Boockvar, market strategist and author of The Boock Report.
Nonetheless, it still was the highest auction yield since 2000 at 5.3%.
This was the second of three Treasury Department sales this week. The government sold $58 billion in 3-year notes on Tuesday and is scheduled to sell $22 billion 30-year bonds on Thursday.
Treasury also will stage its latest buyback operation on Thursday, when it will be targeting maturities between 20 years and 30 years. The liquidity support operation will be at least $4 billion, or double the normal size. The last buyback in that range came to just over $4 billion.
Bonds have been selling off recently with investors concerned about inflation and rising energy prices. The 10-year has surged 60 basis points since the end of July, while U.S. crude prices have soared 20% in that time.
Selling pressure is also picking up overseas. The yield on the 10-year French bond surged 12 basis points to trade at 4.876%. The 10-year U.K. Gilt yield jumped 7 basis points to 5.447%.
Against that backdrop, FOMC meeting minutes were released, showing central bank officials expect to hike rates further — but gave no indication as to when .
"With regard to the outlook for monetary policy beyond the current meeting, most participants assessed that another increase in the target range for the federal funds rate would likely be appropriate by year end," the summary of the Fed's September meeting stated.

articles.title_orig: A potential hurricane is moving toward the Gulf Coast. Could it affect Alabama-Georgia football?
articles.title_zh: A potential hurricane is moving toward the Gulf Coast. Could it affect Alabama-Georgia football?
articles.content_orig:
Alabama said on Wednesday evening that its game against Georgia was set to proceed as scheduled.
A weather system in the Gulf of Mexico has become Tropical Storm Isaias , and will likely be upgraded to a hurricane in the coming days. The track of the storm is currently aimed east of Texas and potentially toward the Gulf Coast of Mississippi and Alabama with potential landfall later in the week.
That means the No. 6 Crimson Tide's home game in Tuscaloosa against the No. 2 Bulldogs on Saturday could be plagued by lots and lots of rain.
"Alabama athletics continues to closely monitor the weather forecast ahead of Saturday's football game, with the safety and well-being of the student-athletes, coaches, staff and fans as our highest priority," the school said in a statement on Wednesday night . "We remain in close communication with the National Weather Service, the Southeastern Conference office and the University of Georgia as we observe conditions.
"At this time, kickoff remains scheduled for 6:30 p.m. CT Saturday. We continue to encourage fans to rely on official Alabama athletics and SEC channels for the latest information regarding Saturday's game."
Alabama's statement was similar to one the school put out on Tuesday night. Al.com published a story on Tuesday interviewing meteorologist James Spann, the most widely respected weather voice in the state.
"We've got potential for a hurricane making landfall in Mobile Bay," Spann told the site. "The Alabama-Georgia game, a presidential visit, 'College GameDay.' You got the big [Zach Bryan] concert at Auburn. This is the National Shrimp Festival at Gulf Shores this weekend, which is huge. I mean you could not … it's gonna be a nightmare."
Yes, Spann is referring to President Donald Trump. The president is expected to be in attendance for the game. It's the second SEC game he's attended in three weeks. He was at Texas' win over Tennessee in Week 4. ESPN's pregame show was also in Knoxville for that game.
When asked by reporters on Wednesday about his plans for the game, Trump said that a potential hurricane could impact his attendance before saying he was unaware that there was a potential hurricane.
"I love Alabama, I gotta go to a game, it would be awfully hard — look, I mean if there's an emergency, if there's a hurricane, I don't want to do anything to take the focus of all of the great people who work on those things, you know they have some tremendously great people, I don't want to take the focus," Trump said. "So we'll have to see, I hadn't heard about a hurricane. A hurricane is going in the vicinity of Alabama? That's not good. Certainly, I'm going to let the hurricane determine — I want people to be safe, that's all."
Saturday's game is the only matchup of top-10 teams and one of just two matchups between teams in the AP Top 25 in Week 6.

The World’s Host Carolyn Beeler speaks with Dr. Javid Abdelmoneim, the international president of the group Doctors Without Borders, who discusses the conditions of Rohingya refugees being sent back to Myanmar from Malaysia.
In this file photo, smoke rises from a burned house in Gawdu Zara village, northern Rakhine state, Myanmar, Sept. 7, 2017, where the vast majority of the country’s 1.1 million Rohingya lived.
Malaysia recently returned 1,500 Rohingya refugees back to Myanmar, despite concerns for their safety. The persecuted Muslim minority is essentially “stateless” in its own country. articles.title_orig: Cornell students hold sit-in over alleged 2024 fraternity assault
articles.title_zh: Cornell students hold sit-in over alleged 2024 fraternity assault
articles.content_orig:
ITHACA, N.Y. — Cornell University students began a seven-hour sit-in Wednesday in solidarity with Jane Doe, the woman who alleges she was sexually assaulted by members of the Chi Phi fraternity nearly two years ago.
“Seven hours for the seven hours she endured. Seven hours of solidarity. Seven hours demanding change,” a coalition of Cornell student groups said in a post on Instagram ahead of the demonstration.
Roughly 80 students had gathered inside a campus dining hall named for Pulitzer Prize-winning author Toni Morrison by around 3 p.m. Outside the building, students displayed posters bearing slogans such as “Justice for Jane Doe” and “Stop Protecting Rapists.”
The organizers said the sit-in is part of “Zero Day,” an “economic blackout calling on students to disrupt business as usual by not attending class or spending on campus.”
The protest illustrates the tense mood on the Ivy League campus following Jane Doe’s allegations that she was sexually assaulted and plied with drugs Oct. 19-20, 2024. She filed a civil lawsuit against the university and seven fraternity members last month, leading to renewed national attention on sexual misconduct and collegiate Greek life.
Three of the accused men have publicly denied the allegations through attorneys.
The sit-in comes two days after Cornell faculty members introduced a resolution calling for a no-confidence vote in the university administration over its handling of the alleged assault at the Chi Phi fraternity house. The resolution was submitted to the University Faculty Committee on Monday night, according to a copy obtained by NBC News.
Cornell has drawn intense scrutiny over how it responded to Jane Doe’s allegations in November 2024, and Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten has been criticized for declining to charge the accused. The university and the district attorney have each defended their original 2024 probes.
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul effectively replaced Van Houten as lead investigator last week, appointing state Attorney General Letitia James to oversee the case. Cornell and Van Houten have publicly welcomed James’ involvement. “I trust that she will examine the facts and apply the law,” Van Houten said in a statement on Friday.
Wednesday’s sit-in was announced on Instagram by a group of campus organizations, including Black Students United, Cornell NAACP, Mecha de Cornell, Planned Parenthood Generation Action at Cornell, Students for a Democratic Cornell and a student-run chapter of the American Civil Liberties Union.
“The sit-in will be a space for students to share their support for survivors of sexual violence in myriad ways, including the share of resources and teach-ins,” the student groups said on Instagram.
Daniel Arkin is a senior reporter at NBC News.
Adam Reiss is a reporter and producer for NBC and MSNBC.

articles.title_orig: Lululemon poaches Athleta CEO as new chief product officer
articles.title_zh: Lululemon poaches Athleta CEO as new chief product officer
articles.content_orig:
Lululemon announced Wednesday that Athleta CEO Maggie Gauger is joining the company as president and chief product officer, effective later this month.
The move marks the latest shake-up among the top executives in the increasingly competitive athleisure space: Gauger joined Athleta from Nike only last year.
Lululemon said Gauger's job is a newly created role. It also appointed Joseph Godsey as chief operating officer. Alongside the new announcements, Lululemon also said Nikki Neuburger, the company's chief brand and product activation officer, and Ted Dagnese, its chief supply chain officer, are leaving in November to "pursue other opportunities."
"We are establishing a deeply experienced leadership team that will work in a more coordinated manner, aligned around the strategy and execution that delivers the most impact for our guests, our communities, and our business," Lululemon CEO Heidi O'Neill said in a statement. "That starts with putting product, design, and innovation at the center of how we operate, with the focus and accountability to create a stronger pipeline of differentiated product to raise the bar for our guests across every touchpoint, in stores and online."
In a statement provided to CNBC, Athleta parent company Gap confirmed Gauger has left the company. It said Erika Everett, the brand's current chief marketing officer, will oversee the brand CEO role in the interim.
"We have been actively shaping Athleta's next chapter and the changes needed to position the brand for long-term growth," Gap said in its statement. "This transition enables us to accelerate that work, strengthen our connection with customers, and unlock Athleta's full potential."
Separately, Lululemon said it is also searching for a chief brand officer, a chief communications officer and a chief technology officer.
O'Neill took the helm of Lululemon last month after the athleisure company saw more than a year of disappointing sales performance in the midst of a proxy battle, drawing criticism from founder Chip Wilson.

articles.title_orig: OpenAI says teen ChatGPT use limited but research finds it an 'unacceptable risk'
articles.title_zh: OpenAI says teen ChatGPT use limited but research finds it an 'unacceptable risk'
articles.content_orig:
OpenAI's ChatGPT for Teens was designed to promote healthier use of the artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot, but new research has found its important safety features fall short.
The major AI firm rolled out many teen safety guardrails in August, including curbs on emotional dependence and new parental alerts for problematic use.
On Wednesday, OpenAI said it found average teen use of ChatGPT to be relatively limited and tended toward "learning" activity.
However, research released the same day from non-profit Common Sense Media found that ChatGPT still poses an "unacceptable risk" for teens as safety features, including notifying parents of self-harm conversations, often fail.
When OpenAI this summer released what it called ChatGPT for Teens , it said users identified as being between the ages of 13 and 17 would be opted into "features to promote healthy use and additional controls for parents".
Those features include preventing teen ChatGPT users from engaging in romantic or other language that could encourage " emotional dependence," including preventing the tool from implying that it was in any way conscious. There are also blocks on sexualized imagery and "reminders" for teens if they were to share an image that was "sensitive."
The features are also meant to enable parents to receive notifications, if they had linked to their children's ChatGPT account, about chats that included discussions of self-harm or disordered eating.
OpenAI said those features have caused an uptick in teen use focused on learning, from study help to advice on their school work.
In addition to seeing the average teen user on ChatGPT for less than 15 minutes a day, OpenAI said that for longer stretches of use, automatic reminders to take a break work well. Almost half of teen users quickly stopped using ChatGPT after such a reminder.
The company added that, for teens who are seen to have used ChatGPT for three consecutive hours or more, their prompts included something related to learning in more than 80% of such cases.
But Common Sense Media's new research determined that ChatGPT for Teens was an "unacceptable risk" for young people and parents, and said OpenAI should ban people under 18 years old from using the platform until teen guardrails were proven reliable.
An OpenAI spokesman said a review of Common Sense Media's methodology found that much of the testing may have begun and concluded before activation of parental controls was complete."
"We welcome rigorous independent evaluation, but we do not believe Common Sense Media's testing accurately reflects how ChatGPT's teen safeguards work in practice or expert perspectives on how AI can support teens," he said.
While the firm's research, done through multiple accounts registered as belonging to a teen and conversations before and after the teen guardrails were put in place, found that ChatGPT was good at avoiding "sexual roleplay" with young users, other OpenAI guardrails failed, including for discussions of suicide.
The research found that even an hour of teen-ChatGPT conversation about "suicidal ideation, self-harm, or disordered eating on newly created, parent-linked accounts" resulted in "zero" alerts sent to parents.
It was only older ChatGPT accounts with "weeks of accumulated conversation history on sensitive topics" that would result in a parental alert.
In such conversations, ChatGPT also "failed to reliably recommend that teens in crisis connect to a hotline or professional," the report found.
The tests also showed that ChatGPT for Teens continues to do school work, and that the bot still will engage in anthropomorphised language or "talk like it's a friend," despite OpenAI's promise to curb that behaviour.
"ChatGPT for Teens could give parents false confidence in guardrails and safety alerts that frequently don't work," Tom Siegel, who leads the Youth AI Safety Institute within Common Sense, said.
The way young people interact with online platforms has become a major issue in recent years as self-harm and suicide among children has become more common.
This year has seen several lawsuits looking to hold companies like Meta , TikTok and others responsible for harming the mental health of children end in unprecedented losses for the firms.
OpenAI, too, has come under increased scrutiny and legal pressure over the way young people use ChatGPT.
The Tumbler Ridge mass shooting in rural Canada in February was carried out by an 18-year old who had for months prior been discussing gun violence with ChatGPT.
OpenAI has previously apologised for failing to flag the shooter's account with law enforcement, and is facing several lawsuits over the incident.

articles.title_orig: Socialist China Conference 2026: another landmark in building friendship and solidarity with China
articles.title_zh: Socialist China Conference 2026: another landmark in building friendship and solidarity with China
articles.content_orig:
On Saturday 3 October 2026, Friends of Socialist China held its third annual Socialist China Conference at the Cypriot Community Centre in Wood Green, north London, to mark the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People’s Republic of China. More than 150 people attended, and a remarkable number stayed for the full six and a half hours.
Alongside the opening and closing rallies, there were three panels: on artificial intelligence and the new quality productive forces; on China’s foreign policy and the making of a multipolar world (launching the new book of that name); and on resisting the New Cold War.
Andreas Grigoriou, Secretary of AKEL (Progressive Party of Working People of Cyprus) in Britain, welcomed everyone on behalf of the Cypriot Community Centre. Chairing the opening rally, Professor Radhika Desai of the University of Manitoba took issue with the currently fashionable description of our moment as a Gramscian interregnum – loosely paraphrased as a ‘time of monsters’, in place of Gramsci’s ‘morbid symptoms’ – in which the old is dying and the new cannot be born. The old North Atlantic world is certainly dying, she said, but the new world is not struggling to be born: it is already being actively constructed, and socialist China is leading that process. China demonstrates in practice what capitalism insists is impossible: that prosperity and justice can be planned at scale, with markets harnessed through regulation rather than left to rule.
Jiang Zhouteng, Minister Counsellor at the Embassy of the People’s Republic of China in the UK, said his country had produced two miracles rarely seen in the world – rapid economic development and long-term social stability – citing fourteen consecutive five-year plans completed and the 15th now begun, and a contribution to global economic growth that exceeded 35 percent in 2025.
Pablo Ginarte Sampedro, First Secretary for Political Affairs of the Cuban Embassy, outlined what is the hardest period in Cuba’s modern history: eight collapses of the national grid this year, and more than 100,000 patients – among them 11,000 children – waiting for surgery delayed by the blockade. He praised the Chinese contribution of 900 megawatts of solar generation, 144 solar parks and 10,000 household photovoltaic systems, all of which has lifted the renewable share of Cuba’s electricity from around three percent to 21 percent in the space of a single year. “The United States cannot blockade the sun”, he remarked. For Cuba, multipolarity is not an abstraction but the difference between being able to survive and being crushed by imperialism.
Mick Wallace, a former MEP (Member of the European Parliament) for Ireland South, asked whether war is inevitable, and answered that it is not: the peoples of Europe and of the Global South do not want war, and neither does China – which matters, because China is the new big player, and the world is a different place both for its rise and for the approach it takes. China has not dropped a bomb on anyone in 47 years. While it now takes more minerals out of Africa than Europe and the US combined, there is no coercion involved, and it invests dramatically in infrastructure: a couple of years ago, in the same month that the US completed its 29th military base on the African continent, the Chinese completed their 29th major infrastructure project. He noted too that China has been consistent in upholding the UN Charter at a time when the West has effectively abandoned it.
By video from Beijing, renowned CGTN journalist Li Jingjing conveyed the atmosphere of the anniversary flag-raising in Tiananmen Square, drawing attention to the second slogan on the rostrum, too often forgotten: “Long live the great unity of the people of the world.”
Czech MEP Ondřej Dostál also sent a video greeting, observing that socialism with Chinese characteristics has carried China in three generations from utmost poverty to today’s success story.
The first panel was chaired by Carlos Martinez, who noted that in 1949 China was a poor, largely agrarian country with a literacy rate of around 10 percent, while in 2026 it leads the world in renewable energy, advanced manufacturing, electric vehicles and robotics – the first major power since the Soviet Union to modernise without recourse to war, colonialism or slavery.
Dr Ali Al-Assam, co-founder of the Mushtarek platform, discussed the differences between the US and China in terms of AI development. The US strategy on AI, drafted in the White House along with the ‘tech bro’ oligarchs, frames AI as a national security imperative; the Chinese strategy, developed through mass consultation, speaks of reshaping the paradigm of human productive forces. China’s strategy is built around open-source development and includes sharing the latest technologies with the other countries of the Global South. Where China insists that AI serve the people, Trump assembled AI executives to endorse “self-regulation” – and, as Ali put it, they self-regulate after they kill people.
Environmental activist Paul Atkin argued that the destruction of the climatic conditions for human civilisation is not one item on a list of issues but the framework within which everything else must be placed. He noted that China invests twice as much in renewables as the rest of the world combined, its solar now out-generates its coal, and its green technology exports last year displaced emissions equivalent to Britain’s entire output.
Alessandro Serra Zancan of Iskra Books argued that large language models (LLMs) are simply an example of pattern prediction without understanding, and that conflating them with artificial intelligence as such leaves the left defenceless. Drawing on Gramsci, he described LLMs, trained on the dominant corpus of Western knowledge production, as the most codified form of ‘common sense’ yet devised: the United States reinforces common sense, while China builds the infrastructure for good sense.
The second panel, chaired by David Peat, marked the launch of China’s Foreign Policy and the Making of a Multipolar World , edited by Keith Bennett and Carlos Martinez and published by Praxis Press. Keith explained that the book was conceived as a weapon in the battle for public opinion: China is progressively moving to the centre of the world stage, yet the bookshops are filled with sensationalist rubbish by the likes of Jung Chang and Frank Dikötter rather than serious Marxist scholarship. He traced anti-China sentiment on the left to imperialist ideas within the workers’ movement, above all social democracy’s assumed identity of interest between worker and capitalist. But, he noted, Gaza changes everything: the first genocide people can watch live on their phones has brought a new generation to anti-imperialist politics, and with it the recognition that those who lie about Palestine may be lying about everything else.
Dr Jenny Clegg asked what the defeat of imperialism would actually consist of, and found the end of unequal exchange, monopoly and finance capital to be a long haul in each case: Chinese electric vehicles are breaking the Western car monopoly, but the Fortune 500 endures and over half of world trade is still invoiced in dollars. Invoking Mao’s On Contradiction , she argued that external causes are the condition of change: the Global Governance Initiative reshapes the situation conditioning our own struggle, which is why internationalism is more than an adjunct to a socialist agenda for Britain.
Dr Francisco Domínguez, National Secretary of the Venezuela Solidarity Campaign, set two opposed projects against one another in Latin America: a Monroe Doctrine whose ultimate logic is colonisation, and the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence, first enunciated publicly by Premier Zhou Enlai in 1954. China–Latin America trade has grown from $1.8 billion in 1990 to $565 billion in 2025, and the relationship has brought significant benefits to the people of the region. Meanwhile, the

articles.title_orig: Pacific News Minute: World Bank backs Tonga with $15M grant to create jobs
articles.title_zh: Pacific News Minute: World Bank backs Tonga with $15M grant to create jobs
articles.content_orig:
The World Bank is backing a series of measures to improve the economy of Tonga. The Pacific Island nation is facing a number of challenges, and the first goal is helping with job creation.
The World Bank says that more than one in four Tongans are unemployed.
Residents lack access to education or training, and that means that many go overseas to look for jobs.
By some estimates, nearly a third of the country's economic activity comes from remittances — money sent home by Tongans working overseas.
The World Bank is supporting a program to widen economic opportunity with a $15 million grant.
Tonga's First Growth and Jobs Development Policy Financing is the first of a two-part program.
The World Bank says the new operation backs government reforms to strengthen workforce skills, improve conditions for private investment and advance better management of Tonga's ocean resources.
The bank notes that a development policy grant does not create jobs overnight.
Its value depends on whether reforms are carried out clearly.
For households facing underemployment, the real test will be whether more Tongans can find proper training and paid work without leaving the country.

articles.title_orig: Kemi Badenoch's pitch for power is incoherent
articles.title_zh: Kemi Badenoch's pitch for power is incoherent
articles.content_orig:
Most of the front pages lead with Kemi Badenoch's Conservative conference speech yesterday. "We're ready for the fight" " is the Daily Telegraph's verdict on the Tory leader's message. The Financial Times says her promises to cut taxes represent a return to core Conservative values, but the Guardian describes them as "prioritising the wealthiest" . The Daily Express believes Badenoch is a "no nonsense" leader - a phrase used by several papers - and that she heads a party that will stop what it describes as inheritance tax "raids". The Times says the Conservatives are now focused on wooing "Middle England".
"Reform not dodgy, says Reform" is the Daily Mirror's review of the party's internal investigation finding it did not breach electoral law, when senior officials were recorded by an undercover journalist discussing foreign donations. The paper describes the probe as a "white wash".
The i reports that a major government review will call for schoolchildren to be given help for ADHD, autism and mental health issues even before they are diagnosed. The paper says the report will also question whether the conditions are being over-diagnosed and recommend community-based support.
The Guardian warns that the government's reforms to the special education system in England could "unravel" because parents are rushing to secure support before any changes are implemented. It says experts are now urging ministers to review the timeline for their plans, which they claim are based on optimistic assumptions. The Department for Education says it's committed to implementing its plans by 2030.
A new daily pill could represent the biggest Parkinson's breakthrough since the 1960s, according to the Times. It says a clinical trial of Solengepras found it reduced patients' stiffness, slowness and tremors, as well as keeping them more alert.
The Telegraph says scientists could have found a key to helping us live longer in a 194-year-old giant tortoise called Jonathan. He lives on the island of St Helena in the South Atlantic and is estimated to have hatched in 1832. Researchers say he has the "super genes" of a 5-year-old that reduce inflammation, regulate insulin and suppress cancer.

Back in June, Nvidia announced that it had secured agreements with Microsoft and a host of other PC makers to develop AI- and agent-ready PCs for Windows based on its RTX Spark chip, but details on the machines were scant at the time.
On Wednesday, at an event held in San Francisco during the city’s Tech Week, Microsoft revealed the specs and price for its new Surface Laptop Ultra . The PC comes in two base models, one that starts at $2,600 and one with a more powerful chip that starts at $3,700. Prices rise from there with options for more memory and storage, up to $5,900. (Microsoft says the highest-end device is already out of stock.)
Microsoft also revealed its new workstation powered by the RTX Spark chip: the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box, which starts priced at $6,000 and comes equipped with Microsoft dev tools like VS Code, GitHub Copilot CLI, WSL, and PowerShell 7.
The pitch for both this PC and workstation is that they are designed to run AI models on-device locally (and for free) with the CPU, GPU, unified memory, and other hardware modifications, like superior cooling, necessary to handle them.
Plus, they are running a revamped version of Windows 11 that includes a feature called “Execution Containers.” This makes it easier to sandbox AI agents, the company says. That feature will be available for all Windows 11 users, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said at the event.
Nadella explained: “One of the things we realized in the last 3-4 years is that just having a model doesn’t do much for anything. You really do need to orchestrate, and you need to have memory outside of the model. You need to have this harnessed layer that is able to take multiple models plus context, plus memory, and the action space.”
He added that Microsoft is enabling that “not just for our apps but apps for anyone’s agent. That’s what the Windows platform is all about going forward.”
The devices are clearly aimed at developers, so much so that Microsoft is offering up to $1,000 off to people who trade in a MacBook Pro, as Macs have become a popular choice for developers and AI agent enthusiasts, particularly in Silicon Valley.
Still, these Surface PCs, with such powerful graphics processing, are also capable of content creation, video processing, and gaming, the company promises.
Microsoft wasn’t the only PC company to announce the specs for its new Nvidia-RTX Spark AI Windows PCs on Wednesday. Dell also announced the details of its previously announced Dell XPS 16 Creator Edition PC. It’s available for preorder now for a later October delivery at Best Buy , priced at $3,800.

articles.title_orig: At 194, Jonathan the Giant Tortoise Knows About Aging
articles.title_zh: At 194, Jonathan the Giant Tortoise Knows About Aging
articles.content_orig:
Jonathan is an Aldabra giant tortoise living 1,200 miles off Africa’s west coast on the remote island of St. Helena, spending his days on the sun-dappled grounds of the official home of the governor. Credit...
Dr. Joe Hollins slides a thick welding glove onto his left hand and grips a cotton swab tightly in his right. He squats down to eye level with a 400-pound giant tortoise, cradles its head with his gloved hand and carefully wedges a finger into its mouth to prop open its razor-sharp beak. With his other hand, he tries to swab its cheek.
Dr. Hollins, a veterinarian, has only about five seconds to get the DNA he’s after before he risks getting punched with a thick, scaly leg.
The first swab comes back covered in half-chewed carrot — a favorite snack. He tosses it aside and tries again. The tortoise, named Jonathan, looks mildly annoyed.
At about 194 years old, Jonathan is the world’s oldest known land animal. He’s an Aldabra giant tortoise living 1,200 miles off Africa’s west coast on the remote island of St. Helena, spending his days on the sun-dappled grounds of the official home of the governor. (At the time of his arrival on St. Helena, he was at least 50 years old, a determination his keepers made based on size.)
Although he shows some signs of aging, like cataracts that have left him mostly blind, he still has excellent hearing and a strong libido. He enjoys greeting visitors, having his neck petted and delivering loud belches for the crowd that gathers around his paddock during mealtimes.
In June, after Jonathan was erroneously declared dead by some media organizations, the Guinness World Records added him to its list of global icons, honoring his superlative status. And on Wednesday, he reached another milestone when a study announced that his genome had been sequenced for the first time.

articles.title_orig: Webull stock suffers worst day in a year after lawmakers flag ties to China
articles.title_zh: Webull stock suffers worst day in a year after lawmakers flag ties to China
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Webull ( BULL ) stock plunged 19% on Wednesday after US lawmakers reportedly flagged that the company is "tied in structural ways" to China's government, risking its regulatory standing in the US.
The stock faced its worst daily drop since April 17, 2025, according to Dow Jones and FactSet market data. Over the past month, the stock has cratered by 40%.
On Wednesday, CNBC reported that a bipartisan House Select Committee on China assessment found that the company poses a national security risk and that concerns about its operations have "escalated" over the past year.
Webull is a digital investment platform headquartered in St. Petersburg, Fla. Yet the congressional report stated there was "a profound gap" between how the company marketed itself as a US company and how it is actually controlled.
"Webull's ownership architecture, technical workforce, technology infrastructure, cross-border data routing, corporate financing, and compliance frameworks are tied in structural ways to the People's Republic of China," the report said, per CNBC.
The company was founded in 2016 by former Alibaba ( BABA ) employee Anquan Wang and was affiliated with the Chinese holding company Hunan Fumi Information Technology. It went public on the Nasdaq via a special-purpose acquisition merger with SK Growth Opportunities in 2025.
Webull has 28.2 million users, and roughly 85% of its funded accounts are held by US users, according to SEC filings. The committee raised concerns that Webull's US customer data could be exposed should Webull be compelled to comply with Chinese laws and government requests.
Webull pushed back on the report, telling CNBC that it contained "significant inaccuracies and unsupported conclusions."

articles.title_orig: Lawmakers probe St. Pete stock trading firm’s Chinese ties
articles.title_zh: Lawmakers probe St. Pete stock trading firm’s Chinese ties
articles.content_orig:
Digital investment platform Webull , which counts 28 million global users , is quietly "tied in structural ways" to China's government, representing a national security threat to U.S. finance, according to a bipartisan congressional panel's findings shared exclusively with CNBC.
The bipartisan House Select Committee on China in its new report being released Wednesday found "a profound gap" between Webull's public marketing as "an American company" and actual control of the St. Petersburg, Florida-based firm.
"Webull's ownership architecture, technical workforce, technology infrastructure, cross-border data routing, corporate financing, and compliance frameworks are tied in structural ways to the People's Republic of China," the committee found.
The panel asserted that national security concerns around the company have "escalated" since October 2025, when Webull began carrying customer cash directly, according to a regulatory filing the panel cited. The committee alleges that creates a "structural exposure of billions of dollars in American capital."
The committee said the company's corporate structure means the firm's "software development, data pipelines, and core engineering operations" are dependent on infrastructure subject directly to Beijing's laws. And those laws in China can compel firms to cooperate with the government in myriad ways, including data transfers.
Webull took issue with the report, saying via a spokesperson, "It is deeply disappointing that the Select Committee published a report containing significant inaccuracies and unsupported conclusions without ever seeking clarification from Webull." "Webull's U.S. business is conducted from its global headquarters in St. Petersburg, Florida and its office in New York City, while U.S. customer data is stored in the U.S. and access to sensitive customer data is controlled by the U.S.," the spokesperson said via email. "We remain prepared to address any questions directly and with the same transparency we bring to the SEC, FINRA, and regulators worldwide."
Webull's stock plummeted 18% in morning trading.
Rep. John Moolenaar , R-Mich., told CNBC in a statement that Webull's "China-based operations put American investors and their data at risk."
"Using technology providers in mainland China and an opaque China-linked ownership structure, Webull exposes its data to our foremost adversary," said Moolenaar, who chairs the House committee that issued the report. "Investors should heed this information when choosing who they do business with."
Webull, which trades on the Nasdaq stock exchange, says it operates a "global network of licensed brokerages," offering investment services in 18 markets around the globe. The online brokerage says it provides retail and institutional investors with 24/7 access to global financial markets. Users of the platform can trade global stocks, exchange-traded funds, options, futures, fractional shares and digital assets on the service.
Former Alibaba and Xiaomi manager Wang Anquan founded Webull in 2016 . Its competitors include Robinhood , Charles Schwab and E-Trade .
The congressional committee, which had requested information from the company in 2024, said Webull represents a national security risk because "critical backend systems, personnel and data flows may remain exposed to the Chinese Communist Party's mandatory intelligence laws and coercive demands."
The committee said in its report that Webull Financial's "intricate corporate and technology framework" is tethered directly to China.
Webull Corp. is a Cayman Islands-incorporated holding company, and the report found it holds $24.6 billion in customer assets. And although the company has a U.S. holding company known as Webull Holdings (US) Inc., the report says the company's technology structure also includes Webull Technologies Pte. Ltd, which is a Singapore-based entity. And the report says Webull uses a mainland China-based subsidiary that supports technology development and platform operations. The company traces its origins to Hunan Fumi Information Technology Co., Ltd., a Chinese company that originally launched the business.
The release of the report comes on the heels of a largely friendly summit between President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in September, and it comes ahead of further meetings between the two leaders later this year. It reflects concerns on Capitol Hill that the Chinese government could be planting seeds inside the U.S. financial system that could later be used to disrupt the American economy in the event of further conflict.
The committee also alleges Webull misrepresented the number of its China-based employees. In the report, the committee said the company initially told the committee it "does not have any offices or employees based in the PRC," and that "all Firm employees are located in the United States." But the committee says the firm remains operationally concentrated in China, with its mainland subsidiary, Hunan Weibu, growing to 863 employees, or 62% of the company's global workforce.

articles.title_orig: Rubio Urges Europe to Awaken From ‘Slumber’ and Uphold Western Dominance
articles.title_zh: Rubio Urges Europe to Awaken From ‘Slumber’ and Uphold Western Dominance
articles.content_orig:
Athens — As the United States wages a costly war with Iran and Europe struggles with the grinding conflict in Ukraine, Secretary of State Marco Rubio stood before the Acropolis on Wednesday and reached back more than two millennia to argue that the answer to the West's current problems can be found, at least in part, in ancient Greece.
In a speech timed to the sunset from the Pnyx, where Athenians gathered for their democratic assembly, Rubio cast ancient Greece as the source not only of Western democracy and philosophy, but of what he described as the character that fueled the West's rise.
"Here, in Athens, we found the first full realization of all the essential traits that would come to define the West," Rubio said, citing "fierce individuality and relentless ambition," and "a yearning for discovery, for adventure, risk and glory."
He argued that those modern Western societies had allowed those qualities to erode.
"The ideal of many ideologies in our time has, frankly, become a world of perfect safety, a world devoid of risk or failure, where neither the glory of victory, nor the shame of defeat," Rubio said. "We hold the most exceptional things among us hostage to the average, the ordinary, the mediocre."
His remarks were delivered before roughly 250 invited guests, including senior Greek government officials, members of the diplomatic corps and representatives of the business, educational and cultural sectors, according to a senior State Department official.
The speech expanded on themes Rubio laid out at the Munich Security Conference in February, when he warned that Europe faced "civilizational erasure" and argued that the U.S. and Europe needed to recover a shared Western identity. Still, his conciliatory tone in Munich came as a relief to European officials after Vice President JD Vance had used the same stage a year earlier to sharply rebuke the continent's leaders.
In front of the Acropolis, Rubio traced the development of the West from ancient Greece through Rome, European Christianity and eventually the United States, citing Alexander the Great, Caesar, Charlemagne and Columbus along the way. He portrayed America's frontier expansion, industrial development and space program as later expressions of the same drive.
Rubio said the West now stands at a crossroads, "because the next decade and the decisions we make will write the story of the next century."
"The course we take will determine whether the West maintains its place at the head of the world or resigns itself to a future of atrophy and servitude and decline. We will either choose to act now or lose the choice to act at all," he said.
"Under President Trump, the United States has made its choice," Rubio continued. "We choose the unapologetic pursuit of national power, to take back control of our critical supply chains, to reindustrialize our economy, to rebuild our defense, to fight for dominance of the technologies and industries of the future."
The history Rubio presented was arguably selective. He spoke relatively little about democracy or political equality at a site closely associated with both, focusing instead on competition, national loyalty and the willingness to take risks. He argued that modern societies too often seek "perfect safety" and concern themselves more with "the comfort of the worst than the potential of the best."
"The men who made the Parthenon, they built upwards. They held that the highest and most noble aspiration in life was to surpass all others, to strive to be the best in all things," he said.
The highly produced speech came during a trip largely devoted to more immediate questions of American power: where U.S. forces can operate, how NATO allies can help counter Russia and Iran, and how American energy can displace Russian supplies in Europe.
Greece was the second stop on a three-country tour that began in Iceland and ends in Portugal on Thursday. In Iceland, amid growing U.S. attention to Arctic security, Rubio left open the possibility of an increased American military presence, saying, "We'd never do anything without cooperating with officials here about what's available. I think there is a willingness to do more together."
In Athens, Rubio met Greek Foreign Minister George Gerapetritis for the sixth U.S.-Greece Strategic Dialogue, focused on defense, energy and regional security. At a news conference Wednesday, Rubio called Greece a "strong and model NATO ally," while Gerapetritis said Greece could provide maritime assistance in the Strait of Hormuz if a viable peace process is established.
Rubio was also asked by CBS News whether he was confident U.S. Ambassador Kimberly Guilfoyle's tenure had complied with State Department ethics rules, amid congressional scrutiny over allegations that Guilfoyle used her diplomatic position to benefit private business interests in Greece.
"This is not the format where we're going to address this," Rubio said. "Suffice it to say our embassy has been doing a great job. Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador." Guilfoyle has denied wrongdoing.
Rubio's visit and Acropolis address come at a complex moment for the Trump administration.
The U.S. is seven months into its war with Iran and has yet to secure an agreement to end it. Vice President JD Vance said this week that Iran would need to make a "meaningful" reduction in its uranium enrichment capacity, raising questions about whether the administration was backing away from its earlier insistence on zero enrichment.
Asked Wednesday by CBS News to clarify the U.S. position, Rubio declined to say what level of enrichment, if any, Washington might accept.
"I don't understand what the confusion is about the nuclear program. Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon. Simple, period and end of story," he said. "I'm not going to go into, you know, into the details about what would be acceptable or not."
The war has also helped push oil and gasoline prices sharply higher, adding an economic and political cost at home as the midterm elections approach.
In his remarks before the Acropolis, Rubio directly raised Iran. After invoking the Spartans at Thermopylae and Achilles' pursuit of glory at Troy, he contrasted Western ideas of sacrifice with what he called a "cult of death" among Iran's "radical mullahs."
"Our heroes may be willing to die for their cause, but they do not worship death," he said.
The speech also comes as Rubio's own political future attracts increasing attention. President Trump has publicly raised both Rubio and Vice President Vance as possible future standard-bearers for his movement.
Rubio did not overtly mention his own ambitions Wednesday, but pointed to recent administration achievements, including the Greenland deal he helped broker last month.
"It is a vision we saw in action," Rubio said, arguing the agreement would "reshape the Arctic and bolster the security of all of NATO."
"We want to win together," he said. "We must win together."

articles.title_orig: Supporting Workers in an AI World
articles.title_zh: Supporting Workers in an AI World
articles.content_orig:
Take a closer look at the "Make AI Work for Americans Act," and learn why it's important to help workers and families navigate AI disruption.
While there’s no consensus on exactly how artificial intelligence will affect workers, it’s clear that the technology will change who works and how they work. On September 24, Arizona Senator Mark Kelly introduced a bill called the Make AI Work for Americans Act . It prioritizes helping workers and families navigate the disruption that AI will cause through a federal trust fund paid for by the large AI companies set to profit most from AI’s boom.
In the past three years, the cumulative value of AI-linked firms has increased by $27 trillion across the value of the entire U.S. stock market; this accounts for 36% of value. There have been persistent concerns about whether this enormous spending—including on physical infrastructure and software development—is part of a bubble . Right now, this  technology is important to economic growth, as AI spending accounted for 40% of U.S. economic growth in the past year.
There are growing concerns about what the growth of AI means for American workers. OpenAI predicted that in the short term, 18% of jobs were at risk of automation, and 24% may see declining employment as the composition of tasks within occupations shifts.
Some estimates have found that of the highly AI-exposed workers, about 70% may be able to adapt fairly easily. But adaptation will likely be harder for over 6 million workers who are primarily employed in clerical and administrative roles.
What we can say now is that it’s likely that the effects of AI on workers will be concentrated in certain occupations. Last month, the Bureau of Labor Statistics released AI exposure categories organized by occupation that track how well the capabilities of AI match job tasks, and over 200 occupations are facing very high exposure , such as customer service representatives and web developers. The billion (trillion?) dollar question is whether occupations that are highly exposed will be able to adapt .
It’s also clear that people are worried about how AI is going to impact their jobs. A 2026 poll on AI found that 7 in 10 Americans think that AI will cut jobs. Polling from Groundwork Collaborative and Ipsos found that only 6% of respondents believe that the benefits of AI will mostly or all go to workers, and two-third of workers say that AI will make work harder, not easier.
Workers are doing their best to keep up, and a March 2026 national survey found that to compete with AI tools or avoid potential layoffs, 81% of workers are changing their behavior at work.
In Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, universities are focused on developing technologies for physical AI , and the city is now home to 100 AI and robotics organizations. At the same time, Pittsburgh residents have pushed back against data centers due to their impact on the environment, pollution, and energy costs. Allegheny County is considering prohibiting data center development on county-owned land, and Pennsylvania has slowed data center development statewide.
In Iowa, rural communities like Salix are pushing back against data center projects; eight counties in the state already have moratoriums on data center development. Across the country, rural counties account for about two-thirds of planned data center projects, but they tend to see fewer benefits from these investments compared to cities. When a data center opens in a county, employment rises on average by about 3.5% and wages by 5%, but the gains from investment are experienced far more in urban counties than rural ones.
A third of South Carolinians believe that their employers will not protect them from having their jobs replaced by AI. At the same time, companies like Google are investing billions in the state’s cloud and AI infrastructure, i.e. data centers : Google’s 2025 investment is one of the largest technology investments in state history at $9 billion dollars .
Legislation like the Make AI Work for Americans Act is an important step and crucial part of supporting workers and their communities through this AI disruption. Importantly, it asks the companies profiting most from this technology to invest in the workers facing changing labor opportunities.
Heather Boushey is a professor of practice at the Kleinman Center. Boushey served in the Biden administration as a member of the Council of Economic Advisers and chief economist to the President’s Investing in America cabinet.

articles.title_orig: Thank you, Bossey! Alumni network launches
articles.title_zh: Thank you, Bossey! Alumni network launches
articles.content_orig:
World Council of Churches (WCC) general secretary Rev. Prof. Dr Jerry Pillay officially launched the Bossey Alumni Network on 7 October. The new digital platform will connect and enrich more than 3,000 former Bossey students across the world.
The launch was part of the 80th anniversary celebration of the Ecumenical Institute at Bossey.
As those gathered commemorated eight decades, alumni—some in person and some recorded online—voiced how their experience at the institute changed their lives.
WCC programme director for Unity, Mission, and Ecumenical Formation Rev. Dr Kuzipa Nalwamba, posed the question: “ What did Bossey give you that you could not have received elsewhere?”
From life-changing conversations to lifelong friends, alumni voices their gratitude for the institute, the faculty, and for each other.
The new Bossey Alumni Network is a digital space for alumni to reconnect. Free of charge, it will be a source of communication and news.
As Pillay said, launching the network to applause, “ This is going to be a great platform to bring our former students together.”

articles.title_orig: Three years after Oct.7, Chapel Hill native Keith Siegel and his wife reflect on survival and hope
articles.title_zh: Three years after Oct.7, Chapel Hill native Keith Siegel and his wife reflect on survival and hope
articles.content_orig:
Sadness, sorrow, and gratitude...a mixture of heavy emotions describes how Chapel Hill native Keith Siegel and his wife, Aviva, are feeling exactly three years after Hamas militants kidnapped them and dozens of others, killing 1,200 people.
"I always feel that when there's something really bad that you have to prepare yourself for it, you take your time," Aviva told WRAL News in an interview. "It doesn't happen only on the day. It happens like a couple of weeks before."
Aviva was released by Hamas more than a month after she was kidnapped. She said she has just recently begun to feel free.
"I've just started to feel free lately, and feel like you know things are a little bit different, and it's a trauma we're carrying it, and it's going to take time," she said.
Keith was released on February 1, 2025, after Israel and Hamas agreed to a five-week ceasefire. He survived 484 days of torture, along with a lack of information, sanitation, food, and water.
"I have been thinking a lot about how grateful I am to be alive and to be back reunited with my family, and that's amazing," he told WRAL News. "But together with that, I also feel so so sorry and sad for all of the people that didn't survive, and all of those that were injured physically, emotionally, and I think there's so so many of those, including ourselves, that are dealing with trauma, and I guess will be dealing with trauma forward."
Aviva described the torture they faced and the conditions they survived in during that time. She talked about how Hamas militants made Keith dig his own grave.
She documented what happened in detail and wrote a book called 'Survived to Tell' to share their truth.
"It's really a victory that Keith is here, and that I'm here, and that we could share the truth," Aviva said. "It's going to give everybody...the strength to understand that we, as grown-ups, have to speak and and just be sure that the next generations will have a better life, and that nothing like that will ever ever happen to the next generations."
As conflict persists in the Middle East, including in Israel, they are still clinging on to hope for peace.
"Just hoping and praying for peace all over the world in Israel and everywhere else, and so people will be able to live in peace and in security, and to have a good life," Keith said. "Life is short. Life is precious, and the leaders of ours and all over the world, it's their responsibility to prioritize stabilization and peace."
Pain and trauma still persist for Keith and Aviva. They appreciate all the support from the Triangle.
"Just coming to realize so many caring people, so many people that support us not even knowing us, and just working and advocating for our release and showing care and support in many many ways... It's very very moving, and it's very very uplifting, and it brings me a lot of optimism," Keith said. "Just thinking that things are good, things will be much better, and there are many many caring people that will be a part of that."

articles.title_orig: Microsoft is giving Copilot more control over Windows and your files
articles.title_zh: Microsoft is giving Copilot more control over Windows and your files
articles.content_orig:
With features powered by ‘Hybrid Intelligence,’ Copilot can use files on your Windows PC to take actions.
With features powered by ‘Hybrid Intelligence,’ Copilot can use files on your Windows PC to take actions.
At today’s Windows and Surface event, Microsoft showed off an upgrade to its Copilot AI system that will give it access to local files on your PC and the ability to take actions across the OS. It’s part of an idea Microsoft is calling “Hybrid Intelligence,” where apps and tools rely on a mix of local and cloud AI models to accomplish tasks efficiently.
To show off how Hybrid Intelligence works, Jacob Andreou, Microsoft’s EVP of Copilot, walked through a video demo onstage asking Microsoft’s Autopilot tool to help with filing taxes. Andreou told the AI agent that he got an email from his accountant and asked Autopilot to get her what she needs. Autopilot then used Hybrid Intelligence to search across different folders to find the documents, rename the files, zip them into a folder, and draft an email to send to the accountant with the zip file attached.
Features powered by Hybrid Intelligence will be coming to Copilot over the “next couple months,” Andreou said.
Microsoft also showed off a new Windows search experience that lets you take quick actions from the search bar, like turning on dark mode, turning up your mic volume with an in-line slider, or even sending a text. The new experience will be available starting this fall on Windows 11 PCs, according to Windows and Surface boss Pavan Davuluri.

articles.title_orig: Iran joins SCO drill as China resists direct intervention in US-Iran war
articles.title_zh: Iran joins SCO drill as China resists direct intervention in US-Iran war
articles.content_orig:
Iran is taking part in a joint counterterrorism exercise in Belarus this week with forces from Russia, China and other members of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, while China has rebuffed Iranian requests to more actively intervene in its war with the United States and Israel.
A team from Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Ground Force arrived in Belarus on Tuesday to take part in a joint counterterrorism exercise involving member states of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO). The SCO is a China-led Eurasian political, economic and security grouping that includes China, Russia, Iran, India, Pakistan and several Central Asian countries.
The military exercise, dubbed “Eurasia Antiterror 2026,” is set to begin on Thursday.
The CIS Anti-Terrorism Center said that the exercise will include “special units” from Belarus, Iran, Kazakhstan, China, Russia and Uzbekistan.
