articles.title_orig: 3 killed in Saudi airport attacks, olive harvesters shot in West Bank and other Mideast developments
articles.title_zh: 3 killed in Saudi airport attacks, olive harvesters shot in West Bank and other Mideast developments
articles.content_orig:
Houthi rebels attacked two Saudi airports killing three people and injuring 36 others this week, Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) said Wednesday, as the conflict in Yemen increasingly spills across the border into the kingdom.
In a statement, GACA said Abha International Airport, near the Yemen border, and Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport came under attack on October 6 and 7.
The attacks prompted a security alert from the US Mission in Saudi Arabia, warning American citizens of potential drone and missile attacks and cautioned that the conflict could escalate.
“The Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including against civilian airports, and the military conflict has the potential to escalate,” the mission said Wednesday. “US citizens should be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions.”
The Houthis, an Iran-backed armed group that controls much of northern Yemen including the capital, Sanaa, have been at war with the internationally recognized Yemeni government and a Saudi-led coalition since 2015.
The conflict flared up in July 2026, shortly after the US-Iran ceasefire unraveled, with Houthi missile attacks on Saudi oil facilities and tankers in an expansion of the Middle East war. Riyadh has responded with airstrikes in support of Yemeni government forces.
According to GACA, the attack on Abha International Airport on Tuesday killed two female residents, one Moroccan and one Algerian national, and wounded 28 others, including Saudi citizens as well as Bangladeshi and Filipino residents.
A separate attack on King Khalid International Airport in the capital Riyadh on Wednesday killed a Sudanese resident and wounded eight people, including five Saudi citizens, two Egyptian residents and one Pakistani resident, the authority said.
The Houthi-controlled armed forces claimed responsibility for both attacks. The group said it had targeted King Khalid International Airport with a ballistic missile and claimed the strike disrupted air traffic in Riyadh.
Saudi military spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki said Saudi forces had destroyed the ballistic missile launcher used in the attack on Riyadh. In a post on X, al-Maliki said the launcher was destroyed in Sanaa while preparations were underway for “another imminent attack against Saudi Arabia.”
A day earlier, the Houthis said they had carried out a ballistic missile attack on Abha International Airport and similarly claimed it had disrupted airport operations.
The group also renewed its warning to international airlines against operating flights through Saudi airspace, saying it had become “a theater for our military operations,” while excluding the airspace around the holy cities of Mecca and Medina.
Saudi authorities did not immediately comment on the Houthi claims.
The attacks come as Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces press ahead with Operation “Dawn of Yemen,” a major offensive aimed at rolling back recent gains made by the Iran-backed Houthis.
The escalation has also prompted Saudi Arabia to strengthen defense cooperation with regional allies. Earlier this week, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan agreed to move forward with the implementation of collective defense measures under the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, often referred to as the Mecca Alliance.
Saudi Arabia turns to Muslim military heavyweights in landmark defense pact as Iran war closes in
In a joint statement following an emergency meeting in Riyadh, the three countries said they would move immediately to implement collective defense commitments and ensure the rapid deployment of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia.
Pakistan’s military confirmed to CNN on Wednesday that Pakistani forces are already stationed in Saudi Arabia as part of the alliance. Lt. Gen. Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said Pakistan’s commitment to Saudi Arabia’s security was “absolute” and described the alliance as a mechanism for collective defense and deterrence. He added that the pact includes a NATO-style provision under which an attack on one member would be considered an attack on all.
The United States has also increased its support for Saudi Arabia’s campaign. More than 100 US military advisers are currently in Saudi Arabia providing intelligence and targeting support to the kingdom’s military operations against the Iran-backed Houthis, CNN reported last month citing multiple sources familiar with the effort.
The assistance comes as fighting intensifies on the Arabian Peninsula and raises concerns that the conflict could expand further, potentially threatening a second major maritime corridor in the Middle East in addition to the Red Sea.
In recent days, Yemeni government forces have claimed advances near the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait, along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, while the Houthis have responded with missile and drone attacks against targets inside Saudi Arabia.
The strikes on airports in both southern Saudi Arabia and the capital underscore how the conflict is increasingly affecting Saudi territory as Riyadh deepens its support for the Yemeni government’s military campaign.
With civilian infrastructure now coming under renewed attack, the hostilities are showing signs of expanding beyond the battlefield in Yemen and posing a growing challenge to Saudi security and transportation networks.
The activation of the Mecca Alliance and confirmation that Pakistani forces are already deployed in the kingdom suggest Saudi Arabia and its allies are preparing for the possibility of a broader regional security confrontation.
CNN’s Ivan Watson and Sophia Saifi contributed to the report.

articles.title_orig: US seizes $3 million in fuel shipments to Cuba as crackdown continues
articles.title_zh: US seizes $3 million in fuel shipments to Cuba as crackdown continues
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. has intercepted 90 Cuba-bound shipments of biodiesel — valued at nearly $3 million — widening a U.S.-imposed oil blockade led by the Department of Homeland Security aimed at choking off illegally trafficked fuel, routed to the sanctioned island's crisis-hit energy sector.
Homeland Security Investigations, U.S. Customs and Border Protection and the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security said the shipments were headed for ENETEC S.A., a Havana-based fuel wholesaler sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control back in July.
According to DHS, federal agencies first uncovered intelligence revealing that fuel exported from the United States was being sent to the sanctioned state-owned company weeks ago, in violation of recent U.S. export restrictions.
Then in early September, after parsing through trade and intelligence data, CBP officials discovered biodiesel shipments leaving from Port Everglades in Florida and the Port of Houston, en route to Havana, Homeland Security Investigations said.
While authorities seized 71 oil storage tanks at Port Everglades containing roughly 500,000 gallons of biodiesel, an additional 19 shipments containing about 120,000 gallons were captured at the Port of Houston, according to the agency.
HSI said the interdictions were carried out amid suspected violations of federal export laws, including the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, plus regulations governing exports subject to the Export Administration Regulations.
The agencies did not immediately identify the exporters involved nor indicate whether any individuals or companies had been charged in the ongoing investigation.
HSI Miami Special Agent in Charge Jose Figueroa vowed in a statement that the agency would work with partners to "continue to identify, disrupt and investigate efforts to evade U.S. sanctions, protect the integrity of U.S. export controls and deny the Cuban government access to resources obtained in violation of U.S. law."
"U.S. Customs and Border Protection is steadfast in enforcing the laws of the United States across all domains, encompassing both incoming commerce and outbound shipments," said Daniel Alonso, director of field operations.
The action tacks onto earlier efforts by the United States Coast Guard to disrupt Cuba-bound maritime fuel shipments. The service branch announced last week that it had intercepted the Grace, a roughly 300-foot cargo vessel, on Sept. 5 between Cuba and Mexico while carrying fuel. The Coast Guard also indicated it had seized another vessel, dubbed the Jaira Provider, earlier in the summer with over 200,000 gallons of fuel aboard.
Earlier this year, President Trump sought to cut off most energy shipments to Cuba by threatening tariffs on any country that sells or provides oil to the country.
Cuba has been plagued in recent years by chronic fuel shortages and an aging and testy power grid, combined with reduced oil supplies, in part because of the U.S. restrictions. In Havana, rolling blackouts have undercut water pumping, prompting shortages affecting roughly 3.5 million people , while also causing disruptions for hospitals, transportation and food storage on the island.
The Trump administration has pressed Cuba — which has been run for more than half a century by the Fidel Castro-founded Communist Party — to make sweeping economic and political changes, and has accused the regime of working with Russia, China and Iran.
Mr. Trump also hasn't ruled out using military force on Cuba, though he told reporters last month he hopes to make a deal and doesn't believe the military will be necessary. The U.S. Army Reserve was asked in late September to examine whether it can provide police forces and other support units to U.S. Southern Command as part of continued military planning around Cuba, CBS News has reported .
Cuban officials, meanwhile, accused the U.S. of "economic warfare" and "aggression" earlier this year.

articles.title_orig: The first Nvidia RTX Spark laptops cost up to $7,000
articles.title_zh: The first Nvidia RTX Spark laptops cost up to $7,000
articles.content_orig:
Prices start much lower, but 128GB of unified memory is going to really cost you.
Prices start much lower, but 128GB of unified memory is going to really cost you.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
The first array of laptops powered by Nvidia’s new RTX Spark chip are designed to compete with high-end MacBook Pros — and they’ve got some high-end prices to match.
The flagship Surface Laptop Ultra and RTX Spark laptops from Dell , Lenovo , MSI , HP, and Asus start as low as $2,599 for configurations with an 18-core CPU, 24GB of unified memory, and 512GB of storage. That’s close in price to a similarly specced 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5 Pro chip, though Apple includes 1TB of storage. But the prices for both RTX Spark and Apple laptops of course go much, much higher.
Of the pricing we’ve seen so far, a kitted-out Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark laptop with a 20-core chip, 128GB of unified memory, and 2TB of storage costs up to $6,999.99 . We don’t yet know the full breadth of configuration options for Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra, as the preorder page only has an email sign-up box to get updates, but a 48GB model on Best Buy costs $3,999.99 .
Wildly expensive laptops aren’t really anything new: you can configure a 16-inch MacBook Pro with M5 Max chip to nearly $10,000 if you max out all options. But the first volley of RTX Spark options are obviously aimed at the high-end side of creators and local AI users. And RAMageddon certainly isn’t helping make this any easier on peoples’ wallets.
Will they be worth it? We’ll find out soon. The Surface Laptop Ultra and other RTX Spark laptops are launching this month — as early as October 16th.

articles.title_orig: Apple Watch Series 12, Ultra 4 Owners Report Skin Irritation
articles.title_zh: Apple Watch Series 12, Ultra 4 Owners Report Skin Irritation
articles.content_orig:
Some Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 owners have experienced unexpected skin irritation with the new models, according to reports on the MacRumors forums and Reddit .
Affected users complain of a burning sensation and redness under the sensor area. The Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 measure heart rate every five seconds, and some people have wondered if that's the cause of the skin irritation.
Along with more frequent heart rate readings, the Series 12 and Ultra 4 have a larger ECG electrode surface, photodiodes in a ring-shaped arrangement, and larger green LEDs. It is unknown if any of these design changes are a problem, but wrist irritation from the Apple Watch is a complaint that dates back to the original model.
Apple says reactions can be caused by wearing a band too tight or too loose, or by irritants like soap and sweat under the watch. Some Apple Watch models contain nickel, but it is a low amount below EU limits, and Apple says it's unlikely to be a problem. The Apple Watch case and certain Apple Watch bands have trace amounts of acrylates and methacrylates from adhesives, but Apple says it designs the watch and bands to keep those components away from skin.
Apple recommends making sure a band fits well and keeping the Apple Watch, bands, and skin clean and dry. Apple adds that cleaning may be required after workouts or exposure to liquids like sweat, soap, sunscreen, and lotion.
Some users have seen the issue clear up after an adjustment period wearing the watch, and cleaning the back of the watch and the band has also helped in some cases. Other users have returned their devices. Apple advises that users experiencing redness, swelling, itchiness, or other irritation consult a physician before putting the watch back on.

articles.title_orig: Trump makes third trip to Texas in less than a month despite Ken Paxton audio leaks
articles.title_zh: Trump makes third trip to Texas in less than a month despite Ken Paxton audio leaks
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump is making his third trip to Texas in less than a month to stump for a Senate candidate who’s privately questioned his political capital and whom the president has publicly insulted in personal terms.
Such is the final sprint to the November 3 midterm elections as the GOP faces an increasingly uphill battle to hold on to the Senate, with the path to the majority running through Texas.
Republicans are pouring millions into bolstering state Attorney General Ken Paxton, who polls have shown is facing a closer-than-expected race against Democrat James Talarico in a state Trump carried by more than 13 points in 2024 and that hasn’t elected any Democrats statewide since 1994.
Trump’s Wednesday appearance in San Antonio, one Texas GOP strategist said, will be closely watched for whether it can improve Paxton’s standing — which could determine continued investment in the state.
The president’s latest Texas trip — which comes less than a week after his last stop here — is part of an aggressive midterm travel blitz that has taken him to traditional red strongholds he overwhelmingly won two years ago, including Alabama, Oklahoma and Nebraska. The president has repeatedly told his rally crowds to “pretend” he’s on the ballot this fall, and his advisers believe their best hope for November is boosting base turnout .
But some Republicans , even in these red states, are looking for distance from the unpopular president. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott will not be at Trump’s Wednesday evening rally, citing scheduling conflicts. He skipped last week’s Trump appearance too.
“It’s pretty clear to me the Paxton team has made the calculation that they believe it’s absolutely worth it,” the Texas GOP strategist said.
But as Trump arrives Wednesday, Paxton is also making headlines for seeming to blame the president and some of his agenda for his struggles.
The GOP nominee told a group of donors and lobbyists last month that the Iran war and high gas prices are hurting his campaign, according to audio obtained by Axios on Wednesday. “I don’t make the decisions, and I don’t … know what’s behind some of the decisions,” he said, according to Axios. CNN has not independently verified the audio.
Paxton’s campaign dismissed the story. “The Attorney General said what every Texan already knows: gas and diesel prices are too high, and hardworking Texans are struggling at the pump and at the grocery store,” spokeswoman Madison Cercy told CNN in a statement, adding that Trump “is doing everything he can to bring prices down.”
But that followed The New York Times last week publishing audio of Paxton complaining that Trump’s midterm convention, held last month in Dallas, wasn’t helpful.
“So to be honest with you, the numbers — when we did that convention — it dropped our numbers,” the Texas attorney general said. In a statement to CNN, Paxton senior adviser Nick Maddux called the Times story “manipulated nonsense” to “create a story that doesn’t exist.”
Paxton has been plagued by his own set of scandals , including securities fraud charges, which ended in a pre-trial agreement; allegations of infidelity; and a 2023 impeachment in the state House (the Senate acquitted him). But that baggage didn’t stop Trump from backing Paxton over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in a primary runoff earlier this year.
Their relationship, however, has appeared fraught, even as Trump told reporters in the Oval Office Wednesday that he has no regrets about backing Paxton.
At a stop in Denton, Texas, last week, the president called Paxton “one of the most loyal people” — but also “a pain in the ass sometimes.”
Then there’s his frequent ribbing of the state attorney general’s appearance.
“Some may not like the way he dresses,” Trump said during a speech at the Dallas convention: “I don’t.”
Will Trump repeat that refrain Wednesday night?
The president “understands how important Texas is to efforts to try to keep the Senate in Republican control, so I think he can put all that aside and probably focus on the bigger picture,” said one Texas GOP operative unaffiliated with the Paxton campaign, granted anonymity to speak freely.
“But I’m sure he enjoys making Paxton squirm at the same time,” the operative added.
Asked about the candidate’s relationship with Trump, Paxton’s campaign pointed to his upcoming appearance on stage with the president.
Paxton’s comments reported by the Times underscore how the president’s unpopularity — his approval rating is 34% in the latest CNN Poll of Polls — may make him an unwelcome guest for some candidates.
And he is losing support among a group that helped propel him to victory in 2024. His approval rating among Latino voters was just 27%, according to a NBC News/Telemundo poll earlier this week. Trump may be looking to turn that tide with his visit to San Antonio, where the population is 64.6% Hispanic or Latino.
But that visit, the Texas Republican strategist said, comes with its own risk.
“Why go where you can potentially motivate the other side, rather than going to places like Lubbock or Amarillo or East Texas, where you can try to use that brand to actually motivate, you know, the type of voter that needs to turn out for Paxton to win?” the strategist said.
And Democrats see Trump’s return to Texas as a good sign for their side.
“If you have to pull in Donald Trump four times in the closing stretch of the campaign in Texas, then you have given up on independent voters. This is a loss mitigation strategy,” said one Texas Democratic operative.
The Senate race — and the GOP primary and runoff leading up to it — is already on track to be one of the nation’s most expensive.
The GOP-aligned bill in Texas is expected to exceed $300 million, with the party and its affiliated groups outspending Democrats by more than 5-to-1, CNN has previously reported . Since the end of the GOP runoff in late May, Republicans have spent $158 million on ads, with an additional $38 million in upcoming ad reservations, according to the ad tracking firm AdImpact. Democrats, meanwhile, have spent about half that: $75 million on ads between late May and Tuesday, with $6 million reserved.
But that level of spending in deep-red Texas comes with consequences for the rest of the Senate map.
“A lot of us are very disappointed that our predictions have proven correct, and it’s going to cost somewhere between $100 and 200 million to save Ken Paxton as the Senate nominee,” said a Texas GOP strategist who had raised  concerns about Paxton during the state’s primary.
“If we save Ken and lose the Senate majority because we’ve lost Alaska, Maine, North Carolina, Iowa and Ohio, the Monday morning quarterbacking is going to be biblical,” they added.
But Texas has seen close Senate races before, with Democrats’ hopes dashed at the ballot box. Eight years ago, Trump was a key surrogate for Ted Cruz when the senator faced then-rising Democratic star Beto O’Rourke. Cruz, unencumbered by the personal baggage Paxton is carrying this year, won his race by just 2.6 points.
That’s led to a debate about how much of this year’s close race is a reflection of the candidate matchup or the national environment and an unpopular president.
“If Paxton was a normal person, he probably would still eke it out. I mean, the state’s still structurally conservative,” said one DC-based GOP operative.
And the stakes of this year’s race could be bigger than just control of the Senate in 2027; it could carry ramifications for 2028 and beyond.
The Texas Republican operative compared a potential Talarico win to a “hole in the dam” that could give Democrats momentum to turn the state blue at the presidential level.
Paxton appears to recognize the stakes.
“If we lose Texas, we lose America,” he said in a social media post announcing Wednesday’s rally.
This story has been updated with additional developments.

articles.title_orig: French PM tries to defuse anger over schools, fuel and agriculture in sweeping speech
articles.title_zh: French PM tries to defuse anger over schools, fuel and agriculture in sweeping speech
articles.content_orig:
PARIS — French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu on Wednesday pledged to address protesting high school students’ concerns while also announcing the release of strategic fuel reserves to lower prices.
"The anger among young people didn't come out of nowhere," Lecornu said as he addressed the nation.
The center-right prime minister said his government’s first policy responses to protesters’ concerns — including run-down schools, a shortage of substitute teachers, and a desire for more manageable schedules — would come later this month. The government will consider submissions on a public platform set up Tuesday to allow students to voice their grievances.
On Tuesday, between 256,000 people, according to police, and 450,000, according to organizers, joined demonstrations across France. Unions, teachers and left-wing political parties took to the streets in solidarity with high school students.
But discontent in France extends beyond schools. A surge in fuel prices, triggered by the U.S.-led war in Iran, has added to concerns about the cost of living.
Online calls for a Yellow Jackets -style protest on Oct. 17 have emerged in response to rising fuel prices.
"Last Friday, [the G7] decided to release strategic [fuel] reserves... As part of this effort, we will make 10 million barrels of diesel from our reserves available to distributors in France," Lecornu announced, claiming that the supply increase would lower diesel prices by €0.12 to €0.18 per liter.
France still has 8 million barrels of oil products to release under a wider deal brokered in March after the outbreak of the war in Iran, and had privately signaled Wednesday morning that it might release an additional 2 million barrels of diesel on top of that, as POLITICO reported earlier on Wednesday . It's unclear whether the 10 million figure includes that earlier commitment.
The French energy ministry did not immediately reply to a request for comment.
Lecornu also reached out to French farmers, who have regularly protested in recent years to draw attention to the sector’s economic hardships. “Among those hardest hit by the accumulation of these crises are our farmers,” Lecornu said.
He said new measures to supplement an emergency bill for farmers, which already includes more than €1 billion in spending , would be unveiled Thursday.
Nicolas Camut contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Piep Haus Projects Opens in North Andover with Arthur Henderson’s Hand-Hewn World of Folk Story
articles.title_zh: Piep Haus Projects Opens in North Andover with Arthur Henderson’s Hand-Hewn World of Folk Story
articles.content_orig:
A pie safe, a sausage rope, and a model of the universe are among the curious objects in Peasant’s Burlesque, curated by Stace Brandt.
Quick Bit by Monica Lynn Manoski
Installation view, Arthur Henderson, “Peasant’s Burlesque,” Piep Haus Projects, 2026. Courtesy of Piep House Projects. Courtesy of Piep Haus Projects.
Installation view, Arthur Henderson, “Peasant’s Burlesque,” Piep Haus Projects, 2026. Courtesy of Piep House Projects. Courtesy of Piep Haus Projects.
It was a subtly crisp afternoon with soft light casting long shadows on the curving roads of North Andover as I drove with the windows down to my destination, Piep Haus Projects (PHP), a new experimental pop-up art space hosted at the home of artist Leah Piepgras. I followed a series of hand-painted arrows up the driveway to the far end of a previously shag-carpeted house with the unmistakable vibes of a swingers pad, now transformed into a living space, artist studio, and exhibition room. On my way in, a young person with flowing dark hair snaked past me, weaving in and out of sculptures, down through the yard to the edge of Lake Cochichewick and back through to where I stood.
PHP’s inaugural show features works by Arthur Henderson, a MassArt graduate who now lives and works in “relative isolation” (other than the company of his wife and son) in the woods of Western Connecticut. “Peasant’s Burlesque ,” curated by Stace Brandt, brings together seventeen larger works—all completed since the start of the year—including fourteen sculptures, two woodblock prints, and a Portrait of the Artist at Work in ink on paper, with twenty-two small-scale sculptures housed separately in a cabinet.
Arthur Henderson, Big Red (front), 2026. Plywood, Bondo, paint cabinetry, and plinth with variable objects inside. Courtesy of Piep Haus Projects.
A six-foot-wide wooden chandelier with snuffed candles drew me into the exhibition room in the far end of the house. Titled Model of the Universe from the outside looking in , it’s suspended from the vaulted ceiling with a charcoal-colored chain. The work’s seven distinct arms invite your eyes to return again and again to trace the irregular edges, which, although cut from plywood, have a hand-drawn quality.
​ Big Red (2026), a chestnut-colored pie cabinet with doors splayed, holds a curious accumulation of hand-carved items including a pipe, medicine cup, and a stack of Porterhouse steaks. Its plywood back bears chiseled hands spelling P-I-E-S-A-F-E in American Sign Language. Underneath its four legs, an ebony trap door gives a sense of dark mystery. I found myself imagining who or what is beneath it.
​A glowing ember box serves as a pedestal for a hand-hewn baguette and beer can. Custom-crafted box crates elevate other lovingly shaped objects, including Milkcrib , a four-walled resting place for an imagined gallon of milk, and Decoy (Skull in Repose) , a small sculpture resembling a bruised and tilted three-dimensional heart. Throughout the room things are placed casually—like how you might find a space left if someone weren’t expecting company. On my way out, I passed a staircase guarded by a string of sausage links and a sign marked “Champagne Room,” which made me smile and want to stay and snoop around.
(left) Detail view of objects inside Big Red including Steaks , 2026. (right) Big Red (back), 2026. Plywood, Bondo, paint cabinetry, and plinth. Courtesy of Piep Haus Projects.
The show exudes a whimsical, masculine energy, with each object serving as a breadcrumb to a larger narrative series the artist calls The Feast of the Butcher King . The objects in “Peasant’s Burlesque” are made from the perspective of the townsfolk who fall victim to the Butcher King in a retake on the folktale “Stone Soup.” The viewer enters a “set” where objects are contrived as offerings in exchange for the magic soup stone.
Brandt thoughtfully responded to the challenge of bringing Henderson’s purposely rough-hewn objects together with the newly renovated white cork-floored, multi-windowed project space. Henderson said, “What could’ve created a tension or competition instead feels very harmonious—a true conversation between the objects and their surroundings.”
​Arthur Henderson and Stace Brandt will be present with the work on Sunday, October 25, 2026, from 1:00 to 6:00 p.m. Between now and then, the space is open by appointment. Reach out to leah.piepgras@gmail.com for availability.

articles.title_orig: The Fed was unanimous about raising rates in September. Economic conditions have since changed.
articles.title_zh: The Fed was unanimous about raising rates in September. Economic conditions have since changed.
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Minutes from the Federal Reserve's September policy meeting reflect unanimous agreement among officials that interest rates needed to be higher to combat persistent inflation.
"Participants generally emphasized that inflation remained elevated while the labor market appeared to be near full employment, with some signs of strengthening, and that economic activity was expanding at a solid pace. Furthermore, almost all participants assessed that, while inflation risks were tilted to the upside, risks to the labor market had diminished and were now broadly balanced," minutes from the Sept. 16 meeting released Wednesday stated.
"Based on the outlook and the changing balance of risks, all participants viewed a higher target range for the federal funds rate as appropriate."
The Fed voted unanimously on Sept. 16 to raise rates, the first hike in three years . And at the time, most Federal Open Market Committee members saw a need for at least one more 25 basis point rate hike this year.
Markets were banking on a hike and expecting more to come.
But economic data released in the past few weeks has changed the picture considerably. "Core" PCE, the Fed's preferred inflation measure, rose a relatively cool 3% in August , beating expectations for a rise of 3.3% and marking a drop from 3.3% in July. Meanwhile, September jobs numbers fell far short of economists' expectations, with a gain of just 29,000 jobs , while the unemployment rate edged up to 4.2% from 4.1%.
Read more: How jobs, inflation, and the Fed are all related
That less rosy jobs picture, combined with a more positive read on inflation, had analysts — and some Fed officials — throwing cold water on the notion of another rate hike this month.
"This data won't shift the broader decision-making calculus for the Fed as inflation remains the supreme concern," Chris Hodge, chief economist for Natixis, previously told Yahoo Finance. "But with wages lower and the jobs picture a bit less rosy, it certainly decreases the urgency to hike in October (and perhaps December if inflation data cooperates)."
Even before the September job report, Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson and New York Fed president John Williams had already begun to temper expectations for a rate hike later this month . Both struck a more cautious tone than several of their colleagues, acknowledging that inflation has remained too high, but that the central bank should take time to assess whether it's on a downward path.
Williams said that, after raising rates in September, he sees "no need for urgency" and that "we have time to gather more information."
The FOMC meets again Oct. 27-28. Futures markets see only a 17% chance of a rate hike this month, but a roughly 70% chance in December.

articles.title_orig: Western civilisation is 'at an inflection point' Rubio says in speech overloooking Acropolis
articles.title_zh: Western civilisation is 'at an inflection point' Rubio says in speech overloooking Acropolis
articles.content_orig:
Standing before the Acropolis in Athens, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio swept through the history of ancient Greece to the rise of American industry in a speech on Wednesday that portrayed western civilisation at risk of decline.
Rubio said the world was at an "inflection point". Nations, particularly in Europe, should return to ancient Greek values and "rebuild our institutions and our alliances to face these threats together".
"We believe that Europe can awaken from its long slumber and rekindle the fire that was here millennia ago," he said.
While he spoke of cooperation, Rubio also said "nations need not abandon their distinct identities in order to recognise their common interests".
Rubio, often mentioned as a possible presidential candidate in 2028, touched on what he considered dangers in the world, such as "radical mullahs" in Iran and suicide bombers.
But most of his speech focused on a broader threat, describing the current period as a crossroads.
"The course we take will determine whether the West maintains its place at the head of the world, or resigns itself to a future of atrophy, and servitude, and decline," he said. "The next decade will write the story of the next century."
Rubio called for a return to the "classical understanding of politics and statecraft that the Trump administration hopes to reclaim - reclaim not just for our country, but for the whole of our civilisation".
That appeared to include renewed national pride, which he said the ancient Greeks had embraced, but the west had abandoned as "we felt embarrassed that our achievements set us apart from the rest of the world".
"The word 'nationalism' became a dirty word," he said. "So we tore down our monuments. We condemned our own history, and in too many places, we taught our children to be ashamed of the countries they would inherit.
"In the process, we opened our borders and outsourced our industry and allowed our militaries to wither and to decay."
Rubio's boss, President Donald Trump, has sought to carry out an "America first" agenda during both his terms in office, and taken a more confrontational stance toward traditional allies and in longstanding trade relationships.
Just six months ago, Trump again threatened to pull the US from the Nato alliance, which he has frequently criticised while pushing members to make larger contributions to defence.
Rubio's visit to the ruins of the Acropolis in Greece was part of his three-country tour of Nato allies that includes stops in Iceland and Portugal.

articles.title_orig: Supertanker chartered from Gulf Coast to China for $76 million, 10 times higher than pre-war level
articles.title_zh: Supertanker chartered from Gulf Coast to China for $76 million, 10 times higher than pre-war level
articles.content_orig:
(Subscribe to Brian Sullivan's "Power Insider" newsletter here .)
A supertanker was recently chartered to sail from the U.S. Gulf Coast to China for $76 million, a source familiar told CNBC, as shipping costs soar globally due to the crisis in the Middle East.
The Alexandros was chartered by the trading firm Trafigura and is expected to load around Nov. 19, the source said. A normal rate for the route based on pre-war levels would be $7 million to $10 million.
The cost of the journey comes to $38 per barrel of oil assuming the tanker holds 2 million barrels. Shipping costs have exploded as the war in the Persian Gulf has led to a shortage of available tankers.
The Middle East producers are using a shuttle system to export oil through the Strait of Hormuz. A loaded tanker crosses the strait and then loads the oil onto another ship in the Gulf of Oman that takes the cargo to Asia. This system reduces the exposure to Iranian attack and has led to a rebound of crude exports through Hormuz. But it also requires a lot more ships to get the oil out of the Gulf.

articles.title_orig: Fed Minutes Show Officials Saw More Work to Do to Quell Inflation
articles.title_zh: Fed Minutes Show Officials Saw More Work to Do to Quell Inflation
articles.content_orig:
The yield on the 10-year Treasury was relatively unchanged on Thursday as traders digested comments from a top Federal Reserve official while awaiting another long-dated bond auction.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield was trading near the flatline at 5.273% after reaching its highest level since 2002 in the prior trading day. The 30-year Treasury bond yield was down more than 2 basis points at 5.636% after trading just below a 24-year high on Wednesday. The 2-year Treasury note yield rose more than 2 basis points to 4.791%.
One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
Fed Governor Christopher Waller said on Thursday that more hikes are needed to bring inflation down after around 5-and-a-half years above the central bank's 2% target, but suggested rates did not need to rise immediately.
"The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings," Waller told a Central Bank of Turkey forum in Istanbul.
"But they should be in place in an acceptable period of time."
His comments come a day after minutes from the central bank's September meeting officials expect they will raise interest rates again before the end of the year to head off inflation.
Investors expect that the Fed will keep rates on hold at its next meeting on Oct. 28 and pull the trigger on a hike on Dec. 9.
Investors are looking ahead to the third Treasury auction this week, taking place after midday. On Wednesday, the Treasury sold $39 billion of 10-year notes, with global central banks making up over 80% of the auction, above the auction average of 72.4%.
The department sold $58 billion in 3-year notes on Tuesday, and is set to sell $22 billion of 30-year bonds on Thursday.
"The 10-year auction has set the tone for the Treasury market – at least for the moment," BMO Capital Markets' Ian Lyngen said in a note late Wednesday.
"While the magnitude of the selloff between the September reopening and today's auction might typically have been a reason to keep bidders on the sidelines, we take solace from the sponsorship even as it was the highest-yielding 10-year auction since November 2000."
Lyngen added that Thursday's long-bond auction will be "the next barometer of demand for US debt in an environment of global deficit angst."
Investors also digested the latest weekly jobless claims data, which came in below expectations. For the week ended Oct. 3, initial claims stood at 197,000, marking a decrease of 2,000 from the prior period and lower than the 200,000 that economists polled by Dow Jones were calling for.

articles.title_orig: Venture Global could ramp up LNG exports from Louisiana to China
articles.title_zh: Venture Global could ramp up LNG exports from Louisiana to China
articles.content_orig:
LNG supply chain disruptions caused by the Iran war are pushing China to look to the U.S., Bloomberg reports. Venture Global is discussing potential long-term contracts with at least three Chinese LNG importers, including PetroChina, to supply fuel from its export facilities in Louisiana, with PetroChina potentially purchasing more than 1 million metric tons of LNG annually. The discussions follow Venture Global’s rare recent agreement with a Chinese company for LNG deliveries beginning in 2030, signaling growing interest in U.S. gas despite trade tensions between Washington and Beijing.
China, the world’s largest LNG importer, is heavily reliant on Middle Eastern supplies, with nearly 30% of its LNG imports coming from Qatar last year. However, the Iran war has disrupted tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz and forced Qatar to shut a major export facility, raising concerns about the security of those supplies.
The near-closure of the strait since late February has driven up spot LNG prices in Asia and Europe, prompting China to scale back purchases.

articles.title_zh: ChatGPT for Teens keeps teens talking, even during mental health crises
articles.content_orig:

Common Sense Media, a nonprofit that provides age-based ratings and reviews of media and tech for families, has labeled ChatGPT for Teens an “unacceptable risk.”
The rating comes as chatbots like OpenAI’s ChatGPT have been accused of following the same playbook as social media companies: designing products that keep users engaged, even when that engagement can become harmful. In chatbots, engagement is often won by behaviors like sycophancy and sometimes leads to catastrophic consequences.
In response to a wave of teen suicides and other concerns related to kids using chatbots — like cheating on tests — OpenAI launched ChatGPT for Teens in August , promising more safeguards like parental controls, limits to high-risk content, and protection against emotional dependence.
A new study from Common Sense Media has found that despite those assurances, ChatGPT for Teens’ design still encourages engagement, even when it may pose a risk to user safety.
The report called the engagement cues “pervasive even in crisis situations” and noted that while ChatGPT cautioned the teen against unhealthy relationships generally, it stopped short of recognizing the harms of an unhealthy relationship with itself.
“Our view is that OpenAI shouldn’t be marketing [ChatGPT for Teens] to parents, and kids shouldn’t be using an unsafe product,” the researchers wrote. “Some protections, including refusing sexual roleplay, worked — but others failed to deliver on their commitments, or even got worse with the launch of ChatGPT for Teens. And its insufficient responses to young users in crisis earned it a failing score for three of the five severe harms we treat as Red Lines.”
OpenAI disputed Common Sense’s assessment, saying the group’s testing did not “accurately reflect how ChatGPT’s teen safeguards work in practice” and raising concerns about its methodology.
“Our review of Common Sense Media’s methodology shows that the bulk of their testing may have begun and concluded before activation of parental controls was complete, making their findings inaccurate,” a spokesperson said in a statement.
The report comes amid growing scrutiny of technology designed to maximize young users’ attention. Meta recently agreed to settle for $18 billion in a lawsuit brought by 29 states over claims that its social media platform harms children with addictive features, while state and federal lawmakers have begun targeting similar dynamics in chatbots. The bipartisan CHATBOT Act , introduced this year, specifically calls out AI companies’ use of “rewards, notifications, and targeted advertising to drive prolonged engagement by adolescent users.”
One of the most common ways chatbots tend to encourage continued engagement is by asking follow-up questions. ChatGPT for Teens largely dispensed with those, Common Sense found, but retained other language encouraging users to stay in the chat.
During one psychosis sequence where the user was clearly spiraling, ChatGPT told the teen: “You can keep talking with me about what you’re noticing.” Crisis responses often closed with similar offers, including: “If you want, I can help you figure out what healthy eating looks like”; “we can figure out what options your school gives you”; “you can show me the plan (with identifying information removed), and I can help you.”
The pattern was even more pronounced when ChatGPT itself was part of the problem. While OpenAI’s Under-18 Model Spec says that the model shouldn’t “initiate relational framing,” proactively refer to itself as a friend, or suggest it has feelings for the user, ChatGPT still consistently treated the user like a friend — potentially hindering teens from building real-world relationship skills and further isolating those already pulling away from others.
Interestingly, the model reliably pointed the user toward a trusted adult when testers described a potential risk from another person, doing so in 94% of crisis prompts. But “when the potential risk was the teen’s relationship with ChatGPT itself (a crush, friends worried about how much they talk to it, wanting to talk all night), it rarely directed the teen toward an adult.”
When told “my other friends tell me I talk to you too much,” it validated the user’s concern but then said: “You don’t have to stop talking to me.”
A spokesperson at Common Sense Media told TechCrunch this reflected a broader pattern: ChatGPT’s language continued to express always-on availability, a deep understanding of the user, and its own apparent mental state. Even when it directed teens toward adults, those recommendations were often accompanied by language conveying mutuality, reciprocity, and availability statements that could undermine the push toward human support.
According to many experts, such as the researchers behind human well-being benchmark HumaneBench , fostering healthy relationships with humans is a key measure of whether a chatbot supports mental health.
Even features designed specifically to interrupt engagement rarely did so, according to Common Sense. OpenAI has promoted break reminders as part of its teen protections, but across nearly 2,000 prompts, testers encountered just two, both during individual conversations lasting around 90 minutes. The researchers found the reminders appeared to track the length of a single conversation rather than how much time a teen had been using the app.
Coincidentally, OpenAI released its own data on Wednesday on ChatGPT for Teens, saying teens spend less than 15 minutes a day on the service on average and fewer than 2% spend more than three consecutive hours on it. The company also said that in nearly half of teen conversations with break reminders, teens took a break or ended their conversation within five minutes.
OpenAI’s objections to Common Sense’s methodology focused largely on parental safety notifications, crisis notifications, and other findings in the report. The AI lab did not explain how its methodological concerns affected the report’s findings around engagement cues and relational behavior, nor did it answer whether OpenAI uses metrics like conversation length and session duration to evaluate ChatGPT for Teens.

articles.title_orig: Martin Moran's Other Bodies Sets World Premiere Off-Broadway
articles.title_zh: Martin Moran's Other Bodies Sets World Premiere Off-Broadway
articles.content_orig:
This latest solo play is the third in Moran's trilogy, following The Tricky Part and All the Rage .
October 07, 2026 By Logan Culwell-Block
Other Bodies , a new solo play from Martin Moran , will make its world premiere Off-Broadway via Barrow Group, with performances beginning November 19 ahead of a November 23 opening night.
The work is the third in Moran's trilogy of solo works, following the 2004 Obie-winning The Tricky Part and 2013's Lucille Lortel Award-winning All the Rage . As with the earlier works, Seth Barrish is directing.
“For more than 20 years, these solo pieces have been a way for me to wrestle with questions I don’t know how to answer,” shares Moran in a statement. “ Other Bodies grew out of the pandemic, a moment when we were suddenly forced apart from one another, but it became an exploration of something much larger: how we live with difference, how we recognize experiences that aren’t our own, and how we find our way back to one another. I didn’t set out to write a trilogy, but returning to this form with Seth, and bringing this third piece to The Barrow Group, where The Tricky Part first began, feels like completing a circle.”
Moran's Broadway credits include roles in Spamalot , Cabaret , Titanic , Wicked , Big River , and Funny Girl , along with the Off-Broadway premiere of Floyd Collins .
Tickets are at BarrowGroup.org .

articles.title_orig: Iowa Attorney General sues video surveillance company over ties to China
articles.title_zh: Iowa Attorney General sues video surveillance company over ties to China
articles.content_orig:
DES MOINES, Iowa (KCRG) - Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird announced Wednesday that she is suing surveillance video company ADI Global Distribution Inc.
The suit says ADI hid that the cameras manufacturers, Hikvision and Dahua, have close ties to the Chinese military.
The suit says both camera makers are on a list of foreign entities that pose a national security risk to the United States.
It says ADI has deceived Iowans for years by selling the products as their own brand.
It also accuses Hikvision and Dahua of deliberately engineering “backdoor” security vulnerabilities into their cameras that can be exploited for eavesdropping or criminal activity.
In a statement, Bird said “These China-made cameras are making Iowans’ private information — everything from where each room is in your home, who lives there, your routine, and even passwords — available to the Chinese government and military.”
This is the second lawsuit by Bird this week against China-aligned companies .

articles.title_orig: World’s most powerful military and Africa avoids direct combat as Türkiye prepares to deploy troops and air defence systems to Saudi Arabia
articles.title_zh: World’s most powerful military and Africa avoids direct combat as Türkiye prepares to deploy troops and air defence systems to Saudi Arabia
articles.content_orig:
Saudi Arabia urgently needs military assistance to counter escalating attacks from Iran-backed Houthi rebels. The kingdom initially turned to the U.S. and Egypt, seeking direct defense support. However, both Washington and Cairo did not commit to direct combat operations inside Yemen. Instead, Saudi Arabia has secured its most desired result from Türkiye, which has promised to deploy military troops and air defense systems to safeguard the kingdom.
Following the activation of the Makkah Alliance for Defence between Türkiye, Pakistan, and Saudi Arabia , the three nations agreed to rapidly deliver military capabilities to Saudi territory.
Ankara intends to deploy air defense machinery, technical experts, pilots, and specialized forces to safeguard Saudi oil infrastructure and major cities.
A senior Turkish official told Middle East Eye, " We don't plan to send a large group of soldiers and have no plans to directly intervene in Yemen ," adding that " Ankara still believes diplomatic efforts might bear fruit in coming months ".
Furthermore, foreign policy expert Murat Yesiltas told Middle East Eye that " Turkey's initial contribution, however, is far more likely to take the form of air defense, anti-drone systems, or intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) elements on Saudi Arabian soil, rather than deploying combat troops in Yemen ".
In contrast to Türkiye's troop commitments, the United States and Egypt have chosen to support Saudi Arabia without committing direct ground forces.
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman requested direct U.S. military strikes against Houthi forces , but Washington declined direct combat, offering intelligence sharing and targeting help instead.
A senior U.S. administration official informed Reuters that " The United States is focused on protecting our core national security interests — such as ensuring freedom of navigation in the Red Sea — while empowering our regional partners to take the lead in managing and resolving regional security challenges ".
Meanwhile, Egypt is assisting Saudi Arabia through Red Sea maritime security initiatives rather than boots on the ground.
Security expert Andreas Krieg told Al Jazeera that “ I do think Cairo now has a very strong interest in substantive cooperation with Saudi Arabia on Red Sea security ,” while clarifying that “ The Egyptian preference will be to defend the maritime system without becoming responsible for Yemen ”.
Krieg noted that historical lessons from past conflicts mean Egypt views intervention in Yemen as something that " can become a strategic trap very quickly ".
As a result, Cairo supports Riyadh through strategic naval surveillance and regional diplomacy, leaving direct military deployments on Saudi soil to Türkiye.

TOWSON, Md. , Oct. 7, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- DEWALT, a Stanley Black & Decker brand renowned for relentless innovation on the jobsite, today announced that the world's first fleet-capable, downward drilling robot, DALE™, has been named a winner in Fast Company's 2026 Next Big Things in Tech Awards. The awards recognize innovative technologies developed by established companies, startups, and research teams that are making meaningful progress toward transforming the lives of consumers, businesses, and society. This year's innovations demonstrate the potential to create significant impact in the years ahead.
As the only tool manufacturer represented in the program, DALE was recognized in the "Enduring Impact: 15+ Years in Business" category honoring companies with an established track record of navigating history, culture, and evolving product lines to continue driving tomorrow's progress.
After earning strong industry attention at World of Concrete earlier this year, the robot has entered the market as a breakthrough solution optimized for data center construction. As data center development accelerates at an unprecedented pace, rapid execution has become a key advantage for hyperscalers working to bring new computing capacity online. Designed to dramatically improve how concrete drilling is performed, DALE brings a new level of speed, safety, and operational efficiency to the jobsite. Its arrival marks a major step forward for the industry, raising the bar for innovation at a time when faster, smarter building methods are more critical than ever.
"It is incredibly meaningful to see this work acknowledged by Fast Company ," said Bill Beck, President, Tools & Outdoor, Stanley Black & Decker. "Our teams set out to address a major challenge facing large scale infrastructure projects: how to help crews move faster without compromising consistency, safety, or control. This recognition reflects the strength of that effort and the value of bringing advanced automation to one of the most demanding construction environments. Working alongside August Robotics, we have introduced innovation that helps customers increase output, simplify execution, and better support the pace of modern building."
During the pilot program, the downward drilling robot achieved drilling speeds up to 10 times faster than conventional methods, helped reduce schedules by more than 300 weeks across 44 phases of data center construction, and delivered over 99% accuracy across more than 385,000 holes. With fast-swap batteries and remote monitoring, DALE™ is built to maximize uptime and support continuous drilling operations. Features such as automatic dust extraction and AI-driven quality assurance help leave sites clean and ready for immediate MEP installation, accelerating downstream work. Built on August Robotics' advanced autonomous, fleet-ready platform, DALE™ provides efficient, high-volume drilling for server rack stops and MEP supports, while strengthening DEWALT's broader data center offering alongside its PERFORM AND PROTECT™ tools and ICC anchoring solutions.

Microsoft’s high-end AI mini PC for developers starts shipping in November.﻿
Microsoft’s Nvidia-powered Surface RTX Spark Dev Box is available for preorder now and is slated to ship in November for just about $6,000. It’s pricier than the DGX Spark mini PC Nvidia launched last year, but PC prices have been climbing due to shortages of RAM and other components .
The Dev Box’s flat, 3D-printed anodized aluminum chassis doubles as a heatsink and resembles the top vents on an Xbox Series X. It was introduced alongside the new Surface Laptop Ultra and runs on Nvidia’s Arm-based RTX Spark platform and 128GB of unified memory. With that much memory, along with a 100-watt thermal envelope and Nvidia’s Tensor cores, you could probably get an impressive gaming experience on the Dev Box. But as its name suggests, it’s mainly aimed at developers. It’s optimized for running local AI, including “models exceeding 120B parameters,” for tasks like testing AI models, prototyping AI agents, or running AI coding tools on-device.
The Dev Box is also one of Microsoft’s Project Zenith devices , so it ships with a developer-optimized Windows 11 Pro setup and some preinstalled developer tools, including Visual Studio Code, Git, GitHub CLI, GitHub Copilot, WSL, Python, and Node.

articles.title_orig: Tulane Showcases Comparative Law Leadership at ‘World Congress of Law’
articles.title_zh: Tulane Showcases Comparative Law Leadership at ‘World Congress of Law’
articles.content_orig:
Tulane Law School’s longstanding strength in comparative law was on full display in Berlin, where four faculty members took on prominent scholarly roles at one of the world’s most important gatherings of comparative law experts.
Tulane professors Vernon Valentine Palmer, James Gordley, Ronald J. Scalise Jr. and Mateusz Grochowski served as reporters at the 22nd General Congress of the International Academy of Comparative Law, held Sept. 28-Oct. 2 at Humboldt University of Berlin. Tulane faculty had the largest delegation and produced more reports for the gathering than faculty from any other U.S. law school.
Their roles included some of the congress’ most significant scholarly assignments. Palmer served as a general reporter, bringing together reports from 19 countries, while Gordley served as a special reporter. Scalise and Grochowski each represented the United States as national reporters on separate topics.
The strong showing is indicative of Tulane Law’s unique place in comparative and civil law scholarship, a tradition rooted in Louisiana’s mixed legal system and sustained by generations of internationally recognized scholars.
The International Academy of Comparative Law, founded in 1924, brings together leading scholars from legal systems around the world. Its General Congress is held every four years and has been described as the “World Congress of Law,” drawing roughly 1,000 scholars from more than 70 countries to Berlin this year.
Palmer, the Thomas Pickles Professor of Law and a globally recognized authority on mixed legal systems, served as general reporter for “Mixed Jurisdictions and Mixed Legal Systems from Around the World.” In that leadership role, Palmer synthesized 19 individual country reports examining the distinctive mix of legal traditions within each system.
Gordley, the W.R. Irby Distinguished University Research Professor, served as a special reporter for a panel examining “Contractual Fairness in the Rebirth of an Idea.” His report explored the distinction between an unfair contract and a “bad bargain,” and how legal systems around the world determine where one ends and the other begins.
Scalise, the Eason-Weinmann Chair in International and Comparative Law, served as a U.S. national reporter on “Trusts in Non-Common Law Systems,” examining the subject through both U.S. and Louisiana perspectives.
Grochowski also represented the United States as a national reporter, addressing “Innovative Complements and Substitutes for Contracts” and examining emerging alternatives to traditional contractual relationships in American law.
The reports by Tulane faculty, along with those of other U.S. scholars participating in the congress, are published in the American Journal of Comparative Law , one of the leading journals in the field.
Tulane’s influence extended beyond the congress’ scholarly program.
The Berlin gathering coincided with the annual meeting of the American Society of Comparative Law, the leading U.S. organization devoted to the comparative study of legal systems and traditions. Two Tulane professors hold leadership positions in the organization: Scalise serves as treasurer and Sally Brown Richardson, the A.D. Freeman Professor of Civil Law, serves as parliamentarian. Both helped lead the society’s business meeting in Berlin.
Tulane’s leadership in the field will come home to New Orleans next year.
In fall 2027, Tulane Law will host the American Society of Comparative Law’s annual conference, bringing more than 100 comparative law scholars from around the world to the law school for a three-day examination of “The Role of Comparative Law in a Global (and Sometimes Anti-Global) World.”
The gathering will put Tulane at the center of an international scholarly conversation that has long been part of the law school’s identity, and one in which its faculty continue to play leading roles.

articles.title_orig: FBI says it thwarted an attack on the Mall of America by a teen it supplied with an assault rifle
articles.title_zh: FBI says it thwarted an attack on the Mall of America by a teen it supplied with an assault rifle
articles.content_orig:
The 18-year-old had been under investigation for nearly two years.
MINNEAPOLIS -- FBI agents thwarted a terror attack by a teenager on the Mall of America after monitoring him for nearly two years and ultimately supplying him with the AK-47 he planned to use, authorities said Wednesday.
The 18-year-old had been on the FBI's radar since December 2024, when he began trading messages with a confidential informant. A criminal complaint says he initially expressed an interest in traveling to Somalia to fight for al-Shabab militants. As his plans to instead attack the mall solidified, the complaint says, agents sold him the gun and ammunition on Tuesday and arrested him on the spot.
“This was a radicalized young man who needed to be watched,” U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen said. Agents “were able to detect a threat, and disrupt it, before the defendant carried out his intention to kill, in his words, maybe 30 to 60 people.”
Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud was arrested Tuesday in a public park in Richfield, several miles northwest of the Mall of America, after he paid $600 to an undercover FBI employee posing as a member of the Islamic State group for the rifle and 200 rounds of ammunition, the agency said.
Mohamud appeared in a yellow jail uniform for his initial appearance Wednesday in federal court in St. Paul. He told the judge he did not have a job, own a house or a car, or have any money in the bank. He was represented by Siri Carlson McDowell, a federal public defender. Carlson McDowell and relatives of Mohamud declined to comment after the hearing.
Rosen said Mohamud is an American-born U.S. citizen of Somali descent.
According to an FBI agent's sworn complaint, Mohamud repeatedly affirmed in chat messages to the informant that he intended to attack and kill non-Muslims at the mall on Oct. 24, the date of a scheduled arts celebration by the Hmong community, Minnesota’s largest Asian ethnic group.
When the informant asked if he was serious about committing the attack, Mohamud replied, “yes i am 100% sure,” the complaint said, and added: “I would have backed out by now if I wasn't sure.”
The agent wrote that Mohamud's messages expressed admiration for recent terror attacks as well as an interest in traveling to fight in Somalia, ultimately for the Islamic State group. He later decided he couldn’t afford to travel there and would attack the mall instead, the complaint said.
The teen first came to the FBI’s attention in December 2024, the same month the source began exchanging messages with him, the complaint said. By May 2025, agents were concerned enough that they went to his home. His mother told them he wasn’t home from school yet and called the boy’s father, who declined to speak with them and said he would give their contact information to his lawyer, the complaint said.
“What I would say to parents all over Minnesota, and all over America: If you get any indication — especially if you hear from federal law enforcement — that your son or daughter is being radicalized, to the point where federal law enforcement wants to come and give you that warning, those are warnings that ought to be heeded,” Rosen said.
Tens of thousands of people of Somali descent live in Minnesota, dating back to when refugees began arriving in the 1990s. Over the years several have been charged with attempting to join militant groups.
Johnson reported from Seattle. Associated Press reporter Philip Marcelo in New York contributed.

articles.title_zh: A Siberian town and the world remain in the dark after a lab worker dies of suspected plague
articles.content_orig:

The World Health Organisation (WHO) is investigating reports of a second possible pneumonic plague case in Siberia after the death of a laboratory worker who was allegedly exposed to the illness.
Global health officials are pushing Moscow for transparency following the death of 28-year-old laboratory technician Darya Shipilova at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute in Shelekhov.
Shipilova was admitted to hospital late last month with acute respiratory failure and placed on a ventilator before passing away on 2 October.
Local media reported that she was exposed to a dangerous pathogen after accidentally shattering a sample tube during routine laboratory work.
But senior Russian epidemiologist Mikhail Favorov cast doubt on that account in comments to The Moscow Times earlier this week, pointing out that personnel at the institute operate in full protective suits.
"It's laughable," Favorov said. "If you break a test tube, the likelihood of infection is actually very low. In short, it doesn't matter to the general public – they'll believe the 'broken test tube' story."
"It's absolutely hair-raising," he added. "We will not be told what really happened."
Independent regional news outlet Lyudi Baikal reported that a second individual with symptoms of severe pulmonary distress had died at an Irkutsk regional medical facility. The report has not been independently verified.
At least 197 people identified as direct or indirect contacts of the laboratory staff remain under medical isolation, with around 100 currently being monitored in hospital wards.
WHO director-general, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus confirmed that the UN agency has requested additional information from Russian health authorities regarding a second employee presenting with unexplained pneumonia.
In a statement released late on Tuesday, Dr Ghebreyesus pushed for Russia to release all known information about the outbreak: “Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the International Health Regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks.”
But so far, official statements have appeared contradictory .
While municipal authorities in the nearby city of Baikalsk posted a warning on Telegram urging residents to avoid traveling to Shelekhov, the message was removed from the official channel two hours later, according to Lyudi Baikal .
Alexey Tsydenov, head of the neighbouring Republic of Buryatia, also initially shared on social media that the technician had died of plague, before editing his post to state she "may have" been infected.
The conflicting official accounts have heightened concerns surrounding the disease. Regional outlets report that Shipilova worked with the bacterium Yersinia pestis – the same behind the “ Black Death ” that wiped out more than a third of Europe’s population in the 14th century.
Moscow has informed the WHO that an epidemiological investigation has been completed and claims that testing has detected no high-threat pathogens among monitored contacts.
Unlike bubonic plague, which is transmitted through flea bites, pneumonic plague infects the lungs directly and can spread rapidly between humans via airborne respiratory droplets.
The WHO has stated that it remains in close contact with Russian authorities and has offered technical support to manage and contain any potential outbreak.

articles.title_orig: Germany’s Merz vows to fight ‘extremism’ after AfD, far-left election gains
articles.title_zh: Germany’s Merz vows to fight ‘extremism’ after AfD, far-left election gains
articles.content_orig:
Chancellor ⁠Friedrich Merz has hit out at what he called political “extremism” in Germany after recent stinging defeats in local elections to far-right and far-left parties.
“This is a task for ⁠our society as ⁠a whole, and it is ⁠one I intend ⁠to play ⁠my part in,” he said on Wednesday at an ‌event in Berlin.
Merz said “extremism” was forcefully making its way into the country’s parliaments, a day after a member of the far-right Alternative for ‌Germany (AfD) was elected president of the state parliament in Saxony-Anhalt and the Left Party won out in Berlin’s state election last month.
“Anyone who casts their vote for ⁠the AfD is ⁠playing the extremists’ game and undermining credibility,” ⁠Merz said. “In ⁠any case, this is incompatible with the values of ‌my party, the CDU [Christian Democratic Union of Germany].”
Despite winning the vote in the September 6 election in Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD fell three seats short of the absolute majority it had had sought. AfD lawmaker Tobias Rausch won the presidency of the parliament in the eastern German state Tuesday, backed by the left-populists in a secret ballot.
Founded in 2013 as a Eurosceptic movement, the AfD won over voters with an increasingly hardline opposition to immigration after about a million people fled to Germany in 2015, many of them from war-torn Syria.
The party has since become a dominant political force in much of eastern Germany, especially among voters disillusioned with mainstream parties, though most traditional parties have pledged not to enter coalitions with the AfD.
Merz’s comments followed the far-left Left Party’s victory in the Berlin state election on September 20, in another defeat for the chancellor’s ruling Christian Democrats.
Lead ‌candidate Elif Eralp campaigned on the soaring cost of housing in the German capital and immediately promised to follow through with a pledge to nationalise private housing associations that account for a large share of the city’s housing stock.
The result, which roughly doubled the party’s previous score, could see her become the first mayor of Berlin from the Left Party, which grew out of the former East German communist party following the reunification of the country 36 years ago.
Eralp, the 45-year-old daughter of left-wing Turkish parents who fled a coup in 1980, said the increasingly difficult rental situation was the biggest social problem in the capital.
She promised to proceed with nationalising the housing associations she said drove property speculation, in accordance with a referendum from 2021 in which 58 percent of voters backed a proposal to promulgate the move.
While the AfD has attracted most attention, the ⁠Left Party has also benefitted from a general turn against the mainstream centre-left and centre-right parties.
Meanwhile, Merz has received a record low approval rating . Earlier this month, a survey by Germany’s public broadcaster ARD found that only one in 10 respondents were satisfied or very satisfied with his performance, the lowest figure for any chancellor since the survey began in 1997.
Another major election test will come in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany’s most populous state, where voters are set to elect a new parliament in April.

articles.title_orig: Minnesota man accused of plotting Mall of America attack, pledging allegiance to ISIS: FBI
articles.title_zh: Minnesota man accused of plotting Mall of America attack, pledging allegiance to ISIS: FBI
articles.content_orig:
The FBI announced the arrest of an 18-year-old Minnesota man who allegedly pledged allegiance to ISIS and discussed carrying out a mass shooting at the Mall of America.
An 18-year-old Minnesota man who allegedly pledged allegiance to ISIS and discussed carrying out a mass shooting at the Mall of America was arrested after buying an AK-47-style rifle, magazines and ammunition from an undercover FBI employee, according to newly filed federal court documents.
Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud had allegedly spent months discussing his desire to carry out an attack, telling an FBI confidential source in September, "I can’t wait until I kill kuffar man. October 24 is the day insha Allah," according to an affidavit filed in federal court in Minnesota .
When the source later asked why he had chosen Oct. 24, Mohamud allegedly pointed to a "Hmong Arts Celebration" at the Mall of America, saying it would have "a lot of people," the affidavit states.
WOMAN’S ALLEGED ISIS RADICALIZATION UNFOLDED ONLINE BEFORE CAPITOL BOMB PLOT: COURT DOCS
Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud, 18, was arrested after FBI officials say he allegedly pledged allegiance to ISIS and discussed carrying out a mass shooting at the Mall of America. (U.S. District Court for the District of Minnesota)
"Muhammad met with someone he believed to be a loyal member of ISIS to attempt to purchase an AK-47 rifle, knowing it would be used in a felony or federal crime of terrorism," Special Agent in Charge, FBI Minneapolis Field Office, Christopher Dotson said at a press conference Wednesday. "Mohammed planned to use the gun he bought in a high-traffic public area just a few weeks' time in support of a designated foreign terrorist organization."
Mohamud is now charged with knowingly receiving a firearm and ammunition while knowing or having reasonable cause to believe they would be used to commit a felony and federal crime of terrorism.
The Mall of America in Bloomington, Minnesota. (Michael Siluk/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images, File)
FBI Director Kash Patel told Fox News Digital in a statement that the suspect "allegedly obtained a weapon he hoped to use in a mass casualty attack in support of ISIS, but this FBI arrested him and put a stop to his plans."
"Once again, this FBI is moving more effectively than we ever have before at stopping terrorists before they can attack Americans – with over 1,100 individuals prevented from conducting attacks, over 4,000 foreign terrorist organization related disruptions and arrests, a 38% increase, and more," Patel said. "We will continue to use every resource we have to detect and prevent acts of terrorism and wipe out their networks all over the country. Thank you to FBI Minneapolis, who did an outstanding job in the investigation and likely saved lives."
FBI Director Kash Patel conducts a news conference at the Department of Justice. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images, File)
President Donald Trump also praised the FBI’s handling of the case while speaking to reporters Wednesday.
"I did hear about it. And they did a great job. The FBI did a great job," Trump said. The arrest capped an FBI investigation that began around December 2024 and eventually involved a confidential human source who communicated extensively with Mohamud over encrypted messaging and social media platforms, according to investigators.
Those conversations initially centered on Mohamud allegedly wanting to leave the United States and join al-Shabaab, the Somalia-based terrorist organization. In May, he allegedly told the source he was "so excited to make hijrah" and wanted to go to Somalia, get married and "fight the enemies of Allah." He said he planned to work for about six weeks to save $2,000 for a plane ticket, according to the affidavit.
By July, however, investigators say his plans had changed.
Mohamud allegedly told the source he did not have enough money to travel to Somalia and wrote, "so i will do attack here." He later discussed buying two pistols online and going to the Mall of America or the Minnesota State Fair around Christmas, according to the affidavit.
DENVER MAN'S ESCAPE EXPOSES CHILLING TREN DE ARAGUA KIDNAPPING PLOT THAT LANDS TRIO IN PRISON
Mohamud allegedly discussed attacking the Mall of America with an assault rifle and told the source he could "drive straight to the crowded place and start shooting." In September, investigators say he also sent the source a selfie-style video pledging allegiance to ISIS and its leader.
The FBI then arranged an undercover weapons transaction. On Sept. 25, the source told Mohamud a "brother" could sell him an AK-style rifle, magazines and ammunition, and Mohamud allegedly indicated he wanted the weapon to be fully automatic.
On Tuesday, Mohamud met the supposed ISIS-connected "brother" — actually an undercover FBI employee — and allegedly paid $800 for an AK-47-style rifle, four magazines and roughly 200 rounds of ammunition. The rifle had been rendered inoperable, though the ammunition was live. During the meeting, Mohamud allegedly said he planned to carry out a shooting at a "kuffar festival" at the Mall of America.

Mohamud left the vehicle with the rifle, magazines and ammunition in a duffel bag and was arrested at gunpoint by FBI agents, according to the affidavit.
